items.sum: Stage-by-stage account of the London to Brighton Relay of April 13th, 1935, won by Belgrave ahead of Birchfield, each stage written by a different member.
items.s: THE BRIGHTON RELAY, April 13th, 1935. Stage-by-stage account of the London to Brighton Relay of April 13th, 1935, won by Belgrave ahead of Birchfield, each stage written by a different member. Bert Lindsey begins our "running" commentary. Once again an enthusiastic crowd gathered in Palace Yard, Westminster, to see the start of yet another tussle for supremacy on the Brighton Road. Bill Rice again took this stage for us and as the representative of last year's winning team received the letter of greeting from Sir S. Killick, Lord Mayor of London, to Councillor S. G. Gibbons, Mayor of Brighton. Big Ben (Westminster's, not ours!) began to chime and the 21 starters anxiously waited for the signal to start. Then came the first stroke of eleven o'clock, and they were off! The dash over the first few hundred yards found Bill in the second half of the field, but quickly getting into his stride and (as he himself said afterwards) striving to get his body balanced with the baton, he settled down. This balancing problem was solved, however, by Joe Binks relieving him of it! Apparently, Bill did not intend to let it get far out of sight, for he began overhauling the runners in front, and by the time Batttersea Park was reached the gap was being closed. Meanwhile two bus loads of supporters were waiting at the change-over point on Clapham Common, hoping that Bill would place us in a good position. Suddenly the runners appear, but for a few moments no sight of the familiar claret and gold. Then along comes Bill, in third position, only 25 seconds behind Stansbury (S.L.H.), who had finished on the shoulder of Forryan (Birchfield). Rice had given our team an excellent start, and had run very strongly, particularly in the last two miles, and now we settled down for an exciting race. Our Assistant Hon. Sec,, E. A. Duffett, "relays" the next stage Jim Ginty now took over from Bill and went off about 150 yards behind the leaders. He soon settled down to his job of picking them up; and slowly, but surely, began to overhaul his two opponents. The South London runner was soon shaken off, but the Birchfield man did his best to hang on to Jim's shoulder. Nearing the change-over, however, Jim, with his powerful yet effortless stride, drew away from his rival and handed over the baton to Harry with a lead of 7 seconds from Birchfield. Jim's performance was one of the high-lights of the day, and his time of 26 mins. 34 secs. bettered the Club record for this stage by 13 seconds. Well done, Jim! Tommy ("Nine-in-Six") Scrimshaw takes over the pen. Owing to traffic lights our 'bus was unable to be at Mitcham for the second change-over, but the news that Harry Shields had been given a lead by Jim Ginty was very encouraging. Our first glimpse of Harry was just before the Gas Works, Croydon, and he was then running down the middle of the road looking very determined, and full of running. Hackett, of Birchfield, a very long striding runner who was following Harry, seemed to be having a bad time, but going up the hill just before Purley, Hackett started to overhaul Harry. By now it could be seen that Harry's effort was telling on him, but he stuck to it in his usual dogged fashion. However, Hackett caught him just at the top of the hill. A ding-dong battle then started, with Hackett taking a lead of about four yards down the hill to Purley. After turning right at the bottom of the hill, with about 200 yards to go for the change-over, Harry put in a supreme finish to catch his man, and hand over a lead of about a yard. Well run, Harry! Our Hon. Treasurer subscribes his quota. Jack Flower was our next baton carrier, and started off with the breath of the Birchfield man, J. W. Powell, who has distinguished himself in Midland athletics, hot on the back of his neck. So the two ran throughout the stage, never more than a yard apart, but at the change-over point the yard was still to our advantage, and the baton was still in our possession. Well held, Jack! Arthur Penny, with the scent of wintergreen in his nostrils, the light of battle in his eye, the desire to be up and doing in his heart,—but unfortunately, with his foot in plaster—does the next best thing, and "writes" a stage. We can safely say that the fifth relay is the most critical one in the whole Brighton Relay and this year we entrusted it to Tom Carter, who soon had an old friend and opponent in Webster on his shoulder. Running against a man of such high reputation is enough to worry anyone, but Tom strode on unperturbed, and relentless in the knowledge that he had Webster "licked." Carter gradually drew away, and at Horley we had our greatest lead since the race had started. Well done, Tom! Charlie Jones, sixth man in our journalistic team, takes us from one "pub" to another; metaphorically speaking, of course! Dan Patience now carried on for us from the "Chequers," Horley, to the "George," Crawley, with a lead of 16 seconds over Kibble (Birchfield) who went hard after him, trying to reduce the gap. Both were running very strongly and, it appeared were evenly matched. Next came Poly. H., 23 seconds behind, then S.L.H., and Surrey A.C., who passed S.L.H. on this stage We overtook Dan about a mile from the finish and he was still holding his own. Then we waited for him some way down the road and gave him vocal encouragement of varying degrees of hoarseness—led by Cecil Penny, and ably backed up by Harry Shields. Dan finished strongly, having had a hard run to stave off the challenge of Kibble, who in fact gained only one second. Good work, Dan! Now Tom Cotton carries on the thread. Syd Ring, unfortunate in not running last year through injury, takes the be-ribboned baton. He has about 70-80 yards lead at the take-over and the young Birchfielder goes after him at a terrific pace; rather unwisely, we think. Comrade Ring, however, has a 4½ mile plan and is not greatly concerned with what the young pursuer is doing. As we lose sight of them they are climbing a slight hill. The Stag-bearer has gained a little, but is expending energy unwisely in this early effort and Syd is doing what a leader must do—running to "schedule." The result? Why, our man has gained 15 secs. on the stage and clipped 7 secs. off Club record (his watch, not mine!) for this stretch. Well run! G. S. Doubleday, dubbed "Doub," on duty. The eighth stage has the greatest drop of all, about 400 feet, but there is a "bump" of 150 feet after descending Handcross. Alf Taylor took the baton and made a good pace downhill, and the Birchfield man, S. G. Smith, was seen to be running very strongly in the rear. We passed Alf going uphill, and our hopes in him were strengthened when the angle of his feet was pointed out! Although our lead was slightly diminished on this stage, our man was second fastest (Smith being fastest) and he is to be congratulated on having recorded such good time against many capable opponents, especially as he made his own pase throughout. Up the hill, Alf made a magnificent burst to hand on the baton to Bert Footer. Joe Flower pens the penultimate stage. Our Captain had a lead of 16 seconds given to him, and he set about his job with his usual determination, and although faced by a head-wind, recorded 28 mins. 51 secs. for this stage, acknowledged to be the hardest stretch in the race. Bert has run in this race more times than any other competitor, and has always put up a good show. It is a pity that his new job prevents him training in the systematic way to which he is accustomed, otherwise it is a safe bet that he would have put up fastest time over the stage. However, after a really hard run he handed on the baton 17 seconds ahead of Birchfield. Well run, Bert! May you lead the boys to yet another win on this famous road next year; and so, with three successive wins set up a record which has yet to be accomplished! The Hon. Editor takes over here to bring our relayed comments of the Relay to a finish. Arthur Allum sped on his way to Brighton, with 6 miles 904 yards to go, a 17 secs. lead, and a downhill and level run! Behind, Whitehouse, of Birchfield, trying desperately to carry his club into the lead and avenge that clear-cut cross-country defeat. The excitement is intense. We try to check our gain or loss every few yards, but might just as well save ourselves the trouble. The Birchfield man's enthusiasm (maybe over-enthusiasm) seems to help him to gain a few yards in the first mile. He cuts across from one side of the road to another in an endeavour to save inches, but the effort is telling, and nothing can rob us of victory now. Arthur Allum is running superbly. We pass through the portals which denote that we have entered the Borough of Brighton. Four miles to go, and our man is drawing away. Three miles to go and our lead is longer; two miles more only and Birchfield are well in the rear. The Belgrave Anthem startles the crowded streets, and the Brighton populace are treated to yet another win by Belgrave. They must be getting used to it now. Relay or Walk, it's just the same! And so to the finish with Arthur still in splendid trim. He has gained twenty seconds on the last stretch, and we are winners of our second Relay after one of the most exciting relays ever. We are proud of our win, for we know that Birchfield have done their utmost to turn the tables on us; and we honour them for paying us this compliment. We are proud of our team; grateful to the reserves who were trained ready to fill the breach if need be, and to all those loyal Clubmen who helped, be it in ever such a small and humble way. Finally, we are all proud to be Belgrave Harriers, and glad to have had the opportunity of participating in another historical occasion when the Club has so grandly distinguished itself. Little has been said of the other clubs taking part; but, quite frankly, from the half-way mark we had little opportunity of studying their progress. The full result is appended. The journey home was very much like any other journey home. The usual stops were made, the usual cordial greetings exchanged, and the usual end came, as come it must. We could hardly have had a better day, so let's hope for many more like it! Stage Name h. m. s. 1 (4 miles 1408 yds.) W. A. Rice — 24 37 2 (9 miles 1584 yds.) J. Ginty — 51 11 3 (15 miles 680 yds.) items.sum: Report and result of the Club 20 miles walking championship for the R. W. Ricketts Shield, won by Fred Rickards for the fourth time, with Ben Clark winning the sealed handicap.
items.s: THE CLUB 20 MILES WALKING CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the Club 20 miles walking championship for the R. W. Ricketts Shield, won by Fred Rickards for the fourth time, with Ben Clark winning the sealed handicap. Percy Wright lifts—the pen, and writes on Fifteen walkers faced the starter for the annual race for the "R. W. Ricketts" Shield, and although there were many notable absentees, including the holder, Tommy Green, one saw enough to convince us that we had a very fine chance of victory a fortright later in the National at Chingford. Our usual course was used, consisting of two laps of the large field of the Common, then along Parkside to Roehampton, returning almost to the finishing point, thence a lap of the "hills" (part of our 7 miles course), and repeating these two laps to complete the 20 miles. From the start Jack Field cut out the pace, opening up a distance of 50 yards in the first mile from Bentley, Bidgood, Harley, Martin, Speechley and Rickards, all of whom appeared unconcerned at the pace set by the leader. At five miles, Field had still further increased his lead. Passing Lauriston Road on the return from Roehampton (8¼ miles) Martin and Speechley had fallen away slightly, but after a lap of the hills, positions had changed considerably. Rickards and Bidgood had now gone into the lead, followed by Field, Bentley, Harley and Martin. The race was now developing in earnest, and the spectators settled down to see a great battle. They were not disappointed, for the leaders were now crowding on pace, and began to open up a gap from Bentley, who had gone into third place. On the way back from Roehampton, at about 16 miles, Bidgood had a lead of a yard or two from Rickards, but of the two the latter looked the more comfortable. So it proved, for on the return from Copse Hill, it was seen Rickards was about 20 yards in front, and before the finish, increased it to fifty yards. Bentley was four minutes away, third; and Harley the same distance away, fourth. Heartiest congratulations go to Fred Rickards, who first won this event eleven years ago, this being his fourth victory. I think a special word of praise should be given to Jack Bidgood, who surprised everyone by his brilliant and determined walking, also to our popular Hon. Secretary, who walked exceptionally well when one considers his so recent indisposition. The sealed handicap was won by a new member, Ben Clark, who should develop into a fine distance walker. Snell took second prize, and Bidgood a well-deserved third. It was pleasing to see Oscar Horwood with us once again, and although he was obliged to retire after eight miles, we hope to see him again before long. Next year one hopes that some of our shorter distance men like Don Brown, Treacher, the brothers Churcher, and others, will venture out in this race. The same group have been our mainstay for a long time, and we cannot always expect them to be there when wanted. So let's see some of the younger brigade making their debût next year! Also started—O. items.label: April-May 1935
items.sum: Report of the R.W.A. National 20 miles walking championship of May 11th, in which Belgrave were beaten for the team title by Surrey Walking Club by one point.
items.s: THE R.W.A. NATIONAL 20 MILES CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the R.W.A. National 20 miles walking championship of May 11th, in which Belgrave were beaten for the team title by Surrey Walking Club by one point. A glorious day with a cooling wind blowing. A large crowd of spectators, a very pleasant course well mapped out to enable the public to see a great deal of the race, and the culminating battle between Belgrave and Surrey Walking Club, which will remain in the memory of many for years to come, briefly sums up the National Walking Championship on May 11th. From the team point of view it was the most exciting race for many years and although beaten by our old friends and rivals, we were certainly not disgraced. Last year they beat us by two points, this year one point, next year —— well, we have asked them to take great care of the trophies for us. We offer no excuses, for our boys walked splendidly. At the outset Wilson (Sheffield) cut out a brisk pace. At the end of the first lap (6½ miles) the leaders were Wilson (Sheffield), Henderson (Worthing), Collier (L. Vid.), Christie-Murray (S.W.C.), Tommy Green (Bel.), followed by Plumb (Enfield). A little farther back were Bentley, Bidgood, Rickards and Joe King, all walking together. It was as early as this that Jock Martin was having a struggle, suffering from a touch of sunstroke, but manfully keeping going. Jack Field was laying handy and Bro. Bert was having a social with Alf Harley. At this point we led S.W.C. by 45 points, the positions being: 1 Bels, 2 Leicester, 3 Sheffield, 4 S.W.C. Tommy was now sixth, walking like a winner. Our next were walking in trio, Bentley 13th, Rickards 14th, Bidgood 15th, and still the team chances looked rosy. Joe King had dropped a bit, Bert Field was 32nd and Alf 34th, but alas! Jack Field had retired. Jack can always be depended upon to give of his best and we know that his retirement was delayed until it was inevitable. Martin was still struggling gamely along, having a terrific battle with himself but determined to finish. S.W.C. had moved up to second team position, but we felt fairly comfortable. At the end of the 3rd lap (15½ miles) the S.W.C. had improved considerably and the excitement was manifest everywhere. A quick and rough reckoning showed us still leading by 3 points. Tommy was still 6th, Bentley and Rickards were now 10th and 11th, while Jack Bidgood was hanging on to the Surrey fourth man in the 16th position. At 18 miles, the S.W.C. had still further improved their position and were now leading by one point! Could we find it? Tommy was now 4th, Bentley 6th, Rickards 11th. Could any of them pick up that point? No, we decided. It couldn't be done here. So Jack Bidgood became the pivot man of the team. Walking well, Jack was still after the Surrey man, determined to catch him; but it was too obvious the Surrey man possessed an equal amount of determination and vitality, for Jack could not make any ground on him. Well walked, Jack! You couldn't find that elusive point, but you gave of your best and we are satisfied. Yes, it seemed here that we were doomed to second place, but wait—who is the Belgrave boy coming along? Good heavens! what speed! Passing man after man and coming up at an incredible pace. Oh! be careful, man, don't get "pulled"! Ye gods! he will almost catch the leaders if he doesn't get pulled "aht." Yes, it is our Percy, running (admittedly) at top speed, sponge in one hand, mother's smelling salts in t'other, and a yell in, or rather "aht" of his mouth, reminiscent of a very Wild West Cowboy making Whoopee. Percy proved himself a very efficient trainer. Well, at any rate he was dressed like one! Grey sweater, flannel trousers (not too clean), white plimsolls (also not too clean), and around his chest (or middle) a sash, girdle, or garter or whatever it was of the Club's colours (so he alleges). He told me afterwards it was the hat band of his old school boater (a very low school), but Percy must have worn a big hat in those days! Anyhow, to get back to the race. Bert Field showed us he is still up to his old form, and Alf Harley maintained his position to the end, although having a bad time over the last 2 miles. Martin had by now recovered a bit and was walking quite strongly. Joe King, who had experienced a bad time at 12 miles, eventually retired in the sixteenth mile. Our second team performed very creditably. Composed of men who have many years of walking in front of them (with the possible exception of Jack Rathbone), they gained valuable experience, and showed that in our reserve ranks we have some who will shortly be qualifying for first team places. Martin has already been mentioned. Stan Goold in his first race for us showed that he will be very useful. Boddington, Snell, Clark and Jarvis all put up creditable shows, as did also C. Hamer, who recently won the M.P.A.A. Novice race, and shows very great promise. We expect much from some of those who constituted our "B" team on this occasion, and we are certain that future seasons will not disappoint us. Five of our men were inside first-class standard time, and three qualify for second-class medals. We were glad to see so many supporters present, and we thank them and hope they enjoyed themselves. One at least—Percy—did. He was suffering from some unknown and mysterious illness in the morning (he showed us her photo at tea-time!) but rather than let down his men he purchased, at great expense (to himself) threepennyworth of Aspros, and was thus able to carry out his duties. e: One Mile Walk for unattached Novices
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes: praise for Jack Bidgood and Tommy Green in the National 20 miles, Len Fletcher training again, the R.W.A. 50 kilos. championship, Fred Rickards's Police championship win, and coming club walks and the novices' mile. You have read elsewhere of the 20 miles Championship. Undoubtedly the hero of the day was Jack Bidgood, who realised that as fourth man it was "up to him" and despite taking a terrible hiding over the last three miles, yet finished gallantly to find we had lost by a single point. Great was his disappointment, but we are sure his reward will come another year. Tommy Green, who was considered "finished" by so many who fail to realise his determination and wonderful ability, gave a wonderful show and proved that he is as good as ever. We trust he will carry on for many years yet. * * * * * It is very pleasing to see an old familiar figure in Len Fletcher out training steadily in Battersea Park. We hope to have him out again with us next season at Wimbledon. * * * * * It has been decided to hold the R.W.A. 50 kilos. Walk Championship, in conjunction with the Bradford Walk, on Whit Monday. No doubt, despite the long distance to be travelled, we shall defend "The Horlick Cup." * * * * * Congratulations to Fred Rickards upon his seventh win in the Barking—Southend Police Championship. He was followed home by two other Belgravians, F. E. Bentley and R. Martin; and many other Belgrave men occupied prominent positions. * * * * * On June 3rd, we hold our Inter-Club Scratch Walks at Battersea Park. As we go to press, the entries are coming in, and it is evident that our competition, with its absence of awards and entry-fees, does not lose in popularity. Future track walks at 2 miles are on Wednesday, June 25th; July 24th; with the Club Championship on August 3rd. Entries and enquiries to the Walking Hon. Secretary. * * * * * On July 29th we hold our annual One Mile Walk for unattached Novices. This event has been the means ol introducing us to many promising walkers, and we should be glad if all members would advise friends likely to be interested. If there's a likely lad in your workshop or office, persuade him to come along. Entry is free, and names should be handed or sent to A. A. Harley. See if it's not possible for YOU to interest one potential walker. items.h: MATCH v. LONDON ATHLETIC CLUB, 1st May, 1935.
items.sum: Report of Belgrave's annual match against the London Athletic Club at the White City on 1st May 1935, lost by 31 points to 25.
items.s: MATCH v. LONDON ATHLETIC CLUB, 1st May, 1935. Report of Belgrave's annual match against the London Athletic Club at the White City on 1st May 1935, lost by 31 points to 25. Our annual match with the London Athletic Club was this year held at the White City owing to the usual date at Battersea Park Track having been altered. It was a very cold evening, and needless to say, the only people in the vast Stadium were the officials and competitors, which made one feel quite lonely when viewing the racing. The L.A.C. paid us quite a high compliment by turning out A. W. Sweeney for the 100 yards, but E. L. Kealey ran quite a good race in finishing second to him. At 50 yards there was nothing in it, but over the finish Sweeney forged ahead. In the Shot Putt our men were well behind the oposition, although Bill Sutton put 34ft. 9in. and should do still better if he perseveres. The 880 yards race saw Tommy Scrimshaw making a welcome reappearance for us and he had some hot opposition in B. F. McCabe, who is, I understand, a quiet tip for the A.A.A. title this year. Tommy, however, dashed away at the gun and, coming round for the first lap, had a lead of 15 yards. His opponent was creeping up and although Tom kept in front until the last bend MacCabe then dashed by to win in 1 min. 59 3-5 secs. The time shows that Tommy is still a force to be reckoned with, and we all hope that he will reproduce the form which gained him many International honours. For the 440 Hurdles we had T. C. Jones, who is an ex-Surrey County Champion, and after a close race he was beaten by a yard or so in 61 1-5 secs. The 2 Miles was easily the most exciting race of the evening. Tom Carter, Jack Flower and Syd Ring were running for us and they had G. H. Vines, the Middlesex Junior C.C. Champion and D. A. Burch, a more than useful middle distance runner, to contend with. For the first mile they kept close company but with a couple of laps to go, Carter went away with Vines on his shoulder, and moreover the latter seemed very comfortable. The bell went, and they tore round the track with Vines doing his best to pass Tom, but this he was unable to do and coming into the straight Tom still held the inside berth. Vines then made the great effort and went slightly in front; but Tom pulled himself together, and with one last burst breasted the tape inches in front. Meanwhile Jack Flower was coming in a comfortable third when Burch came with a terrific sprint, and only just failed to "pip him" for a place. The time, which was 9 min. 54 3-5 secs. was very good considering the wintry conditions; and in Vines the L.A.C. have unearthed a most promising track runner. E. L. Kealey won the 220 yards for the Club, although Sweeney did not turn out for this, but Eddie showed he is in fine form for so early in the season. The 1 Mile race saw J. F. Bain set a very fast pace over the first two laps; and Shaw was lying second after vainly trying to hold on to his man, with Bill Rice still further away, third. With a lap to go, however, Bain seemed to be tiring, and Bill Rice then began to overhaul his man fast. Putting in a fine burst along the back straight, Bill passed his opponent and finished full of running in 4 min. 33 1-5 secs., which really is one of Bill's best performances over a mile. With one event to go we began to count up the points and found that we were only one behind our rivals. The last race was the 440 yards, and Alf Kench and Fred White were our representatives and we felt fairly optimistic. Then somebody told us that the Northern Counties 440 yards Champion, J. W. Anderson, was running for the L.A.C. and so it proved, for Anderson ran a fine race to beat P. J. Halford, also of the L.A.C., in 51 1-5 secs. Alf Kench finished a plucky third, but Fred White seemed to lack the necessary speed and would probably have done better in the half-mile. So, at the conclusion of a very interesting evening's sport, the points were L.A.C. 31 and Belgrave 25, thus reversing last year's result, and we can only hope that next year we shall have yet another of these enjoyable meetings. items.sum: Progress report on Belgrave's Southern Amateur Athletic League Division I campaign, second in the table two points behind Herne Hill Harriers.
items.s: SOUTHERN AMATEUR ATHLETIC LEAGUE, Division I. Progress report on Belgrave's Southern Amateur Athletic League Division I campaign, second in the table two points behind Herne Hill Harriers. Two track events have been decided to date, the 3 miles team race; and 4 x 440 yards relay. Our positions have been second and fourth respectively; and these placings give us second position in the table, two points behind Herne Hill Harriers. We hope to fare well in the four remaining events and repeat our win of last year in the League. The men to represent us were: 3 miles, Ring (4); Carter (7); Allum (10); Ginty (11): and 440 yards, R. G. Michael, J. E. Tosh, T. C. Jones, T. H. Scrimshaw. On the Field Events side we are showing up well. Actual scoring and placings are not available at the moment, but Bill Sutton, our Field Events Captain, fully expects us to run out winners of the competition. He is still anxious, however, to secure some further recruits interested in the jumping and throwing events; so if you know of any young men whose interests lay in this direction, don't fail to bring them along and introduce them to Bill. items.sum: Report of the four-club match at Drayton Green Track, Ealing, on 11th May 1935, won by Belgrave with 35 points to Ealing's 32, Reading 13 and Ashcombe 12.
items.s: INTER-CLUB MATCH AT EALING, May 11th, 1935. Report of the four-club match at Drayton Green Track, Ealing, on 11th May 1935, won by Belgrave with 35 points to Ealing's 32, Reading 13 and Ashcombe 12. The usual four club contest was held at Drayton Green Track on Saturday, 11th May. This year we had newcomers in Reading A.C. in place of Slough A.C., who were unable to field a team so early in the season. The other three clubs were Ealing H., Ashcombe A.C. and ourselves. We were also rather hard put as regards fielding a really useful side, especially so in the sprint races. The 100 yards was divided between Reading, who had first and second, and Ealing, who had third and fourth. Points were scored from four for first place down to 1 for fourth, so that with one race over our score was nil. In the 1 Mile we did rather better and with Harry Shields second and Jack Flower third, we managed to level matters somewhat. The 880 yards saw Jim Tosh turning out once again and he ran in quite his old form in winning in 2 min. 4 3-5 secs. Ealing did well in taking the next three places, although Frank Webb scored a couple of points by filling fifth position. I must explain that in the middle distances points were scored for the first six places. The 220 yards Final was more or less a farce, for to start with, a Reading man together with an Ealing runner were excluded for repeated false starts. This left only two competitors, Brodie, for us, and another Ealing man. At the pistol Brodie shot ahead and was leading upon entering the straight, when the Ealing runner, in making his burst, came a cropper and went on to the grass, leaving Brodie to finish alone. The Ealing man then went past the post but was duly disqualified for leaving the track. So after rather a hectic few minutes we found we had scored four points to the other clubs' nil. The 2 Miles Team race provided our team with an easy win, and the spectators with a view of our crack from Brighton, John Parker. He loped round the track with his tremendous stride and fairly left the others standing. His time of 9 min. 43 4-5 secs. was a new track record, and he certainly made a deep impression on all those present. Alf Taylor had a good race with L. J. Cohen for second place, but was beaten in the run in. Ashcombe rather surprisingly beat Ealing for second place in the team race, Reading being non-starters in this event. The 1 Mile Relay was won by Ealing, who beat our team fairly easily, with Reading third. Upon totalling up the points we found ourselves on top, but only by the narrow margin of 3 points over Ealing, the scores being: Belgrave H. 35 pts., Ealing H. 32 pts., Reading A.C. 13 pts., Ashcombe A.C. 12 pts. items.sum: Report and results of the first Inter-Club Relay Shields contest at Battersea Park Track on 13th May 1935, where Belgrave tied with Mitcham on 13 points, plus two club handicaps; the javelin result prints Deacon's second-placed throw (75ft.) longer than the winner's (55ft.).
items.s: INTER-CLUB RELAY COMPETITION, May 13th, 1935. Report and results of the first Inter-Club Relay Shields contest at Battersea Park Track on 13th May 1935, where Belgrave tied with Mitcham on 13 points, plus two club handicaps; the javelin result prints Deacon's second-placed throw (75ft.) longer than the winner's (55ft.). The first of the contests for the Inter-Club Relay Shields, of which we are the holders, was held at Battersea Park Track on Monday evening, May 13th. Owing to the late appearance of Eddie Kealey, our team in the 4 x 100 yards was not at full strength; and in the circumstances they did well to finish third in a very close finish, with Croydon beating Mitcham for first place. For the 4 x 880 yards we fielded a very useful side, and Jim Tosh gave us the lead over the first stage. Frank Webb went next and was forced to yield the lead to Bidwell, of Croydon; with Mitcham also on our heels, so that for the third stage the three leading runners were together. Fred White put in a good finishing burst and managed to send Tom Scrimshaw away first with a lead of 5 or 6 yards. Naish, of Mitcham, set off after him in hot pursuit, but Tom never allowed his opponent to close the gap and over the last furlong went right away to win easily. Croydon were third, with Epsom a very poor fourth. The 4 x 300 yards was in the nature of a tragedy for us; for with Stroud going first, and Bennett continuing the good work, we saw Michael having a neck and neck race with the Croydon man over the third stage. Kealey was going last for us and so we were expecting to score a win, when to our dismay the Croydon man fell right in front of Michael, who naturally had to stop almost dead, and by the time he got going again, Mitcham had shot away with a 10 yards lead. Kealey rapidly reduced the gap, but on reaching the dressing room the Mitcham lad let it go, and so scored a rather lucky victory for his side. Thus with the 1 Mile Team race to be decided we were 1 point behind Mitcham, but although Thorogood ran a very fine race to win the individual race, we were easily on top in the team race and so managed to level matters, the total scores being: Belgrave H. 13 pts., Mitcham A.C. 13 pts., Croydon H. 9 pts., Epsom H. 5 pts. Two Club Handicaps were decided, and in the 220 yards (under 19) S. C. Botwright ran very finely off the scratch mark to win in 24 3-5 secs. V. D. Wynyard also showed promising form for a boy who is still at school in finishing second, but entries were on the poor side, there being only six starters. In the Javelin Throw, S. Jones deservedly won first prize with A. A. Deacon, and Bill Sutton, filling the minor placings. items.s: OUR MAY SATURDAY MEETING. Report and full results of Belgrave's May Saturday meeting on 18th May 1935, where both Belgrave match teams won (Captain's v. Surrey A.C. and Herne Hill H.; Vice-Captain's v. Leigh-on-Sea H. and Ilford), with club handicaps; Ilford is printed both as Ilford A.C. and Ilford H., and Leigh-on-Sea's all-rounder appears as Seal in the report and Seel in the results. A "double-barrelled" match, supplemented by Club handicaps, was the programme arranged for our meeting on May 18th, and despite a cold cross wind which cramped performances, particularly in the sprints, everything proceeded satisfactorily. We were successful in both match events, the Captain's team scoring 34 points, to the 30 points of Surrey A.C. and 25 of Herne Hill H.; and the Vice-Captain's Team scoring an even more pronounced success by scoring 43 points to the 32 of Leigh-on-Sea H., and 14 points of Ilford A.C. Full results appear below, and I will content myself with a few impressions of outstanding performances. Firstly, it is worthy of comment that all four sprints were won by our men, whereas we were unable to win any of the longer distance track races. Strange, but partly explained by the fact that our first-string middle distance runners were on duty at the White City, fulfilling a Southern Amateur Athletic League fixture. Eddie Kealey showed that we have a front-rank sprinter, although not flattered by the times recorded, and we expect him tto accomplish something really good this year. Stroud and Brodie also showed us some speed; whilst one of our younger members, F. Skelley, gave indication of first-class performances to come. Another young man to call forth our praise was 13-year-old Keith Robertson, who cleared 5ft. 1in. in the High Jump. We shall follow his future progress with great interest. Bill Rice had a nasty fall in the Mile when he seemed all set for a win, but fortunately his injuries have not proved very serious. Scarsbrook beat his club-mate, Nichols, by inches in a stirring finish to the 2 miles event (Captain's Match), and another excellent performance, considering the conditions, was that of George Powell, who threw the Javeli 155 ft. 6½ ins. In the Club handicaps, A. A. Bird (70 yds.) ran extraordinarily well to take the 880 yards event in his first track race. He kept his form right up to the tape, and we are tempted to think that in a year or so he may be showing up well in scratch events. Alec Mewes, another with promise, ran out a narrow winner in the 220 yards handicap, and a third young man, Percy Wright, experienced the pleasure of breaking the tape for the first time in the Walk. Don Brown's 14 min. 7 secs. from the scratch mark on a yielding track calls for superlatives, and we look to him to go near winning an A.A.A. title. E. Foulds won the Unattached Novices Mile in time on which he can easily improve. To conclude, we would call attention to the versatility of R. R. Seal (Leigh-on-Sea) who seemed to bob up in all events, and actually scored 15 of his club's 32 points! We thank our oppo-opponents for two sporting matches, and trust we shall have the pleasure of meeting them again next season. A.A.H. RESULTS. 100 Yards Match (Captain's).—1, E. L. Kealey (B); 2, F. items.sum: Preview of the coming fixtures for Whit Monday to August 1935, including Belgrave v. Birchfield Harriers 3 Miles at the British Games, the Doris Shield, the Inter-Club Relays, the A.A.A. Championships and Club Championship Day, with entry details.
items.s: FORTHCOMING EVENTS. Preview of the coming fixtures for Whit Monday to August 1935, including Belgrave v. Birchfield Harriers 3 Miles at the British Games, the Doris Shield, the Inter-Club Relays, the A.A.A. Championships and Club Championship Day, with entry details. As usual, there is quite a feast of entertainment for Whit Monday, chief among the many Athletic meetings being the British Games at the White City, Shepherds Bush. This meeting will commence at 1-30 p.m. with a Grand March Past of athletes, and will be followed by a gigantic programme of events, including an International Inter-Club contest, and Inter-Universities contest, Open Scratch races at all distances, two events open to those under 20 years of age (i.e., 100 yards and 1,320 yards), and also Relay races. Then, just to give the crowd an exhibition of real running, the Birchfield Harriers and the Belgrave Harriers will compete in a 3 Miles scratch race, with eight men aside to run, and six to count. Whether the "Stag-bearers" can turn the tables on us remains to be seen, but bearing in mind their impressive record for many years past, it is certain that our boys will have to be at the top of their form in order to gain victory. On the same day our old friend, Tom Hampson, is promoting a meeting at Clarence Park, St. Albans, and we have promised to send a team along for the 2 Miles Team race. There are also Open Handicaps at all distances and I hope our members will support these to these best of their ability. On June 22nd there are the Southern Championships at the Royal Naval Barracks Sports Ground, Portsmouth. Whether this venue will prove too far away to appeal to the Metropolitan athletes remains to be seen. Another fact to be borne in mind is that now-a-days you can obtain a Southern Standard medal in your County Championships. I expect, however, that the Varsity men will be there in full force. and if one can manage it, it should be a meeting worth witnessing. On Wednesday, June 26th, at Battersea Park Track, we have the "Doris" Shield Competition between Ashcombe A.C., Thames Valley H., and ourselves. Thames Valley H. are the present holders, and it is up to our boys to bring the Shield back to our safe keeping once again. The events are: 100 yds., 440 yds., 1 Mile Relay and 2 Miles Team Race. These are all level events and points are awarded for the first three places in each race. In addition there are the following joint Club Handicaps: 100 yds., 1 Mile run, 2 Miles walk and Shot Putt. Entries for these should be sent off at once, or handed in at Battersea Park Track on any training night Last year the sprint was very poorly supported by our members and I hope they will remedy this by making this year's race a bumper one. On Saturday, June 29th, we have the S.A.A.L. 1 Mile Team race at the Herne Hill Track in connection with the Civil Service Sports at which are also the following Open Handicaps: 100 yds., 440 yds., 1 Mile, which may be of interest to our members. On Tuesday, July 2nd, at Pampisford Road, South Croydon, will be held the second of the Inter Club Relay contests and if we want to retain our hold on the Shield it is essential that we place a fairly strong team in the field for these away fixtures. On July 6th, at the White City, will be held the A.A.A. Junior Championships, and any members who are eligible to compete should take care to get their entry in early so as to avoid being refused. The following Friday and Saturday, July 12th and 13th, the A.A.A. Championships proper will take place at the White City Stadium. Will all those members who contemplate entering kindly get in touch with the Gen. Hon. Sec., who will submit their names to our Committee, with the object of selecting those who are considered worthy of entry, bearing in mind the special conditions which are now laid down as a condition of entry to these events. On Wednesday, July 17th, at the "News of the World" Track, Mitcham, will be held the third of the Inter-Club Relays, and seeing that this venue is fairly accessible for our supporters I trust we shall see them there in good numbers to give our lads a few shouts of encouragement. On July 24th at Battersea Park Track there will be the following Club Handicaps: 100 yds. (under 16), 100 yds. (Vets. 40 or over), 100 yds. Club, 440 yds., 1 Mile run, and a Discus Throw Handicap. In addition there will be two events Open to all Unattached Novices, i.e., 100 yds. and 1 Mile Walk. These are scratch races and members can help the club by sending their names to our Gen. Hon. Sec. not later than 7 days before date of meeting. Entry is FREE for both these events. Wednesday, July 31st, at Epsom, is the final Inter-Club Relay meeting, and I hope that the members asked to make the journey will do so, and thus avoid our fielding our half-milers in the sprints, as we have so often had to do in the past. Don't forget Saturday, August 3rd, is Club Championship Day at Battersea Park Track. The meeting will start at 3 p.m., and there are championship events at all distances, including the 100 yds. for those under 15 years of age, and the 220 yds. for those under 18. Standard medals will be awarded in all events over the sprint distances and are as follows: 440 yds., 56 secs.; 880 yds., 2 min. 8 secs.; 1 Mile, 4 min. 50 secs.; 2 Miles Walk, 15 min. 30 secs. and 16 mins. Please enter early. You can send your name on a postcard to either of the following, and they will be extremely obliged to all those who do so, and so avoid last-minute congestion. For the Field Events men there will be two Club Handicaps, i.e., Long Jump and Shot Putt. We have not yet instituted Championships for these events although the "Harry Wright" Shield is awarded annually to the best performer in this section. In the past our entries for Club Championships have been sadly lacking in numbers; but I hope that this year, with the deletion of the usual Handicap races, that the members will support the championship events, and thus show that they do not object to competing in company with the Club's so-called "cracks." All Entries and any enquiries can be sent to our— Asst. Hon. Sec., E. A. Duffett, 10, Barrow Road, Waddon, Surrey. or Gen. Hon. Sec., 71 Ravensbury Road, S.W.18. items.s: ANOTHER NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP ! Editorial notes: Belgrave retain the National 50 kilometres walk title and Horlick Cup at Bradford, T. Cotton's Building Fund scheme, a Flannel Dance, the re-opening of Wimbledon headquarters, the coming A.G.M. and unpaid subscriptions. Congratulations to the team which made the long journey to Bradford and successfully defended our title of National Champions in the 50 kilometres Walk, held on Whit Monday. We thus retain the "Horlick Cup" for another year. Tommy Green broke his own record for the Bradford Walk, but finished second to H. H. Whitlock, who caught Tommy in the last two miles. Fred Bentley (6) and Fred Rickards (7) completed our team, and our trio deserve our very heartiest congratulation. The two last-named had anything but an easy journey over the second half of the course; cramp and the severity of the course (the last nine miles of which is reputed to be stiff hill-climbing!) affecting our men, as it did most of the competitors. However, determination got them there, and the final team scoring gave us a one point advantage over Birmingham W.C. Our fourth man, Bob Martin, gained a first-class standard medal. Well done, all! * * * * * Most members have recently received a letter from Mr. T. Cotton, explaining a scheme which can give considerable help to our Building Fund. If the idea is to be carried out, with consequent advantage to us all, it is necessary that the Acting Hon. Secretary be notified immediately of the help you are prepared to give. Much detail work has to be done, and it is essential that the measure of support forthcoming be known well in advance. Please, therefore, make it your duty to write to T. Cotton, 25, Duntshill Road, S.W.18, at once. Many thanks. A Flannel Dance will be held at the Express Dance Hall, Clapham Junction, on Saturday, September 14th, following upon our final track meeting of the season at Battersea Park. Tickets will be available shortly, from our Social Hon. Secretary, and it is hoped that our Social programme will receive a good send-off and thus provide our Social sub-committee with the encouragement to make our 1935-36 season the best yet. * * * * * Our headquarters at St. John's Hall, Ridgeway, Wimbledon, will re-open on Saturday, September 21st. With the mercury high in the thermometer, and our Summer holidays before us, it seems rather strange to be writing of the Winter season—but inevitably Wimbledon days approach. Much as we regret the passing of Summer, many of us look forward to the "country" and the "road," and to all that the Winter season holds in training, racing and cheerful cameraderie. Successful as last season was on the racing side, we can still add a little here and there, whilst not forgetting the very real business of holding what we have. The training part, whatever your rating, whether you profess to be speedy or not, can hold healthy enjoyment for everyone. Our attendance at Wimbledon should not be far short of 200 a week. (We'll find room somewhere! Here, Ben, put Footer on top of the cupboard! Thanks!). The more the merrier. As for the spirit, read K. B. O'Kell (of Ford's S.C. and Belgrave H.) in our last issue. Well, see you there! * * * * * During September, you will receive the customary advice of the Annual General Meeting, which will be held towards the end of the month on a date not yet fixed. Every member should make an effort to be present to hear the account of their stewardship given by the Officials, and to see that those responsible for the management of your Club during the coming season, are those best fitted to do so. It is your duty to your Club, and to the Executive of 1935-1936; for they need your fullest support and confidence if we are to continue to progress. * * * * * And now to end these notes with a constantly recurring subject—unpaid subscriptions. The Hon. Treasurer's heart is heavy and his pocket light (the one in which he keeps the Club money!), and all because a few have yet to fulfil their obligations. To enable the books to be closed for the auditors' inspection, please act at once should you be one of the few who like to enjoy the Club's privileges on a year's credit. This also applies to those who owe for "Belgravians." In fact, all who are indebted to the Club are asked to settle up right away; and if you like to send along next year's subscription as well—do so! The Hon. Treasurer has plenty of receipt books on hand, and nothing pleases him more than to write in your name and the amount, and then sign on the dotted line. Address on page 1. items.sum: Report of Belgrave's annual inter-club scratch walks on June 3rd (five, three, two and one mile races, with results and points; Surrey W.C. won on 122 points, Belgrave second on 105), followed by three Belgrave club handicaps (100 yards, One Mile, Long Jump).
items.s: THE ANNUAL INTER-CLUB WALKS. Report of Belgrave's annual inter-club scratch walks on June 3rd (five, three, two and one mile races, with results and points; Surrey W.C. won on 122 points, Belgrave second on 105), followed by three Belgrave club handicaps (100 yards, One Mile, Long Jump). Our usual programme of inter-club scratch walks was held on June 3rd, and we were accorded splendid support by the Metropolitan clubs, no fewer than ten teams participating. A high standard of walking was seen, generally, and the success of this annual no-entry fee, no-award contest once again confirmed our opinion that this is one of the most eagerly-awaited track events of the season among walkers. Proceedings commenced with the five miles race and Redman (Met.) took the lead followed by Len Fletcher. Later Hake (S.W.C.) came through, and in the latter stages of the race a great duel was fought out between Redman and Hake, the first named prevailing by a few yards. Fletcher finished in third position in 38min. 41sec., which indicates that he is regaining some of his form of a year or so back; and our other representative, Charlie Churcher, finished in fifth place. Totalling the points for this event, we found that Surrey Walking Club and ourselves had both scored 34 points, the next highest being the Valentine's S.C. with 29 points. RESULT. 1, F. Redman (Met. W.C.), 37 min. 42 sec.; 2, H. A. Hake (S.W.C.); 37 min. 44 sec.; 3, A. L. Fletcher (Bel.), 38 min. 41 sec.; 4, F. C. Ryder (Val.), 39 min. 18 sec.; 5, C. E. Churcher (Bel.) 39 min. 48 sec.; 6, L. Woodcock (S.W.C.), 40 min. 1 sec. Fourteen finished. Ashcombe A.C., nil; Belgrave H., 34 pts.; Essex Beagles, 13 pts.; London Vidarians W.C., 11 pts.; Metropolitan W.C., 27 pts.; Poly. H., 24 pts.; Surrey A.C., 9 pts.; Surrey W.C., 34 pts.; Valentines S.C., 29 pts.; Woodford Green A.C., 8 pts. Next came the Three Miles race, and here we saw A. A. Cooper, in action. Harry Churcher was not far behind at the end however; and our other man, Bill Treacher, paying special attention to style, took sixth position. The combined walking of our men gave us a two points advantage over Surrey Walking Club, an advantage we also held in the competition at this point, for we had scored equal points on the first race. Not for the first time, the contest looked like being a neck and neck affair between our Surrey friends and ourselves, although Woodford Green scored heavily in this race. RESULT. 1, A. A. Cooper (W.G.), 22 min. 2 sec.; 2, H. G. Churcher (Bel.), 22 min. 12 sec.; 3, N. L. Burt (S.W.C.), 22 min. 42 [?] sec.; 4, A. H. Foster (W.G.), 22 min. 52 sec.; 5, H. H. Whitlock (Met)., 22 min. 59 sec.; 6, W. A. Treacher (Bel.), 23 min. 2 sec. Fourteen finished. Ashcombe A.C., nil; Belgrave H., 34 pts.; Essex Beagles, 9 pts.; London Vidarians W.C., 11 pts.; Metropolitan W.C., 16 pts.; Polytechnic H., 13 pts.; Surrey A.C., 15 pts.; Surrey W.C., 32 pts.; Valentine's S.C., 22 pts.; Woodford Green A.C., 37 pts. In the next event, the 2 Miles, we were represented by Speechley and Harley, whilst Surrey W.C. had Fisher and Burgess, the Kent champion. From the start Stone (Poly.) led, followed by the Surrey pair, and our two. It seemed that our two points lead was to be taken from us in this event, and we should be all-square on the competition total, leaving the One Mile race to be the deciding event. This was not to be, however, for Charlie Speechley suffered disqualification and we were points down: Surrey W.C. scored 37 points to our 17, and our chance was gone! RESULT. 1, V. W. Stone (Poly.), 14 min. 46 sec.; 2, W. L. Burgess (S.W.C.), 15 min. 23 sec.; 3, M. J. Fisher (S.W.C.), 15 min. 25 sec.; 4, A. A. Harley (Bel.), 15 min. 38 sec.; 5, H. Watts (Met.), 15 min. 43 sec.; 6, A. H. Rayner (S.A.C.)., 16 min. 3 sec. Ashcombe A.C., 10 pts.; Belgrave H., 17 pts.; Essex Beagles, 20 pts.; London Vidarians W.C., nil.; Metropolitan W.C., 25 pts.; Poly H., 34 pts.; Surrey A.C., 23 pts.; Surrey W.C., 37 pts.; Valentines S.C., 23 pts.; Woodford Green A.C., nil. Fourth and last came the One Mile race. Here we had Don Brown, fresh from his win in the Surrey County Championship, and Percy Wright, opposed by Hancock and Amer, of S.W.C. Our chance had gone, but our rivalry still continued, and there was still second place in the competition to be consolidated. Brown gained a comfortable win from Hancock, and in a great struggle for superiority over the last hundred yards, Wright, of ours, and Amer, of theirs, both had to "come-out," leaving the leading six as follows:— RESULT. 1, D. E. Brown (Bel.), 6 min. 57 sec.; 2, L. Hancock (S.W.C.), 7 min. 15 sec.; S. H. Reynolds (W.G.), 7 min 23 sec.; 4, A. De'ath, 7 min. 46 sec.; 5, R. J. Crump (L.V.), 7 min. 46 sec.; 6, C. Webster (E.B.), 7 min. 46 sec. Thirteen finished. Ashcombe A.C., nil; Belgrave H., 20 pts.; Essex Beagles, 25 pts.; London Vidarians W.C., 16 pts.; Metropolitan W.C., 28 pts.; Poly H., 25 pts.; Surrey A.C., 9 pts.; Surrey W.C., 19 pts.; Valentine's S.C., 8 pts.; Woodford Green A.C., 32 pts. FINAL PLACINGS. As a last word—our thanks to the walkers who provided the competition, and those who helped to carry it through satisfactorily and contributed to the undoubted success of the meeting. In addition to the Walking events, we held three Club handicaps as follows:— The 100 yards saw our International half-miler, T. H. Scrimshaw competing, and off the 7 yds. mark he scored a good win, with R. G. Michael yet another half-miler, second off 8½ yds. F. J. Skelley, our promising Junior sprinter, secured third place, but the result on the whole does not reflect very highly on the majority of our so-called sprint men. In the One Mile handicap, one of our cross-country Juniors came to the fore, K. N. Wood winning in very fast time off a liberal mark. G. R. Chantler also showed improvement on previous form in finishing second, with A. A. Bird filling third place. Bird's form on the track is full of promise and he is already recognised as one of our regular team men for the Inter-Club contests. The Long Jump handicap was won by F. J. Skelley and his actual jump of 18 feet should encourage him to persevere, as good long-jumpers are few and far between. As Skelley is only 16 years of age, the future looks full of promise so long as he gives plenty of time to those little details which make all the difference in this branch of sport. Max Henchoz gained second place, with A. A. Deacon third. 1. Surrey W.C. 122 pts. 6. Woodford Grn. A.C. 77 pts. 2. Belgrave H. 105 pts. 7. Essex Beagles 67 pts. 3. Polytechnic H. 96 pts. 8. items.s: THIS AND THAT ! Club notes: a coach and cyclist attendants for the London—Brighton Walk on September 7th (Knott Memorial Shield), Belgrave's ninth place in the Kinnaird Trophy, Jim Ginty's narrow defeat by Scarsbrook in the Southern steeplechase, officials barring J. Parker from the Kinnaird 3 miles (contrasted with D. Finlay's club switching), news from B. C. Button in New South Wales, the narrow British Games team-race defeat by Birchfield, open team race wins, A.A.A. Championships performances and a proposed club points trophy, protest at Ginty's non-selection for England v. France, and the Club Outing to Frensham Ponds. Take notice that we shall have a double-deck coach accompanying the London—Brighton Walk, on Saturday, September 7th. The race has been brought forward a week from the previously advertised date at the request of the Brighton authorities. The race will start as usual at 7 a.m., and our coach will leave Westminster at 7-30 a.m. and proceed by easy stages to Brighton, the return journey being timed for 6 p.m. We shall be strongly represented and expect to win the "Knott" Memorial Shield for the fourth successive year. Tommy Green will be renewing his acquaintance with this race, and Fred Bentley is another we expect to get near eight hours for the journey. Seats on the coach may be booked right away (5/- each) and application should be made to the Walking Hon. Secretary. Last year the number of supporters was very disappointing. Let this year make up for it! * * * * * Offers to act as cyclist attendants to our men during the race would be gratefully accepted by Mr. A. A. Harley. Efficient and conscientious attendants can mean so much to the men they help, and we hope the usual volunteers will come forward and assist our walkers on this occasion. * * * * * We had the usual invitation to compete in the "Kinnaird Trophy" Competition at the White City, and, as usual, our men acquitted themselves well, although scoring but few points. Tom Scrimshaw ran brilliantly to finish second in the 880 yards race; and Syd Ring finished fifth in the 3 miles event. These two men placed us ninth of the twelve competing clubs. Achilles won with 52 points, and the clubs we succeeded in leading at the finish of the competition were Birchfield H. (1), Highgate H. (4) and Mitcham A.C. (1). As we have pointed out repeatedly in these columns, this form of competition places a very high premium on outstanding individuals, and shows but little reward to the Club with a large number of "good average" strength members No doubt, however, the day will come when we shall make a serious challenge to hold the trophy. Certainly, next year, with our added Field Event strength and improved form on the track, we should exceed seven points, which is our best score to date. * * * * * At the same meeting Jim Ginty essayed his first attempt at the Two Miles Steeplechase (Southern Championship), and ran so well that he forced the A.A.A. and Southern Counties champion to run much faster than he did in last years A.A.A. championship. Scarsbrook and Ginty fought it out in the last hundred yards and our man had to admit defeat by a narrow margin. Well run, Jim! * * * * * There was one unpleasant and entirely unnecessary happening in the Kinnaird Trophy Competition. We refer to the action of some of the officials in not allowing J. Parker to run for us in the 3 miles event. Parker had been entered by our Asst. Hon. Secretary (who is probably the most conscientious man in England in regard to entries) according to the terms of the entry form, which were that all members were first-claim members of the club they were representing. As Parker had been a member of our Club for more than three months he was obviously eligible to compete for us in an individual event. However, at the instigation of some of the other competitors, in some strange fashion team race rules were said to apply to an individual event. And, in still stranger fashion, the Judges said it was so! One is amazed at such "reasoning," and is tempted to ask if, when Team Race rules were first introduced, anyone had suggested that they could be so construed, would he not have been covered with ridicule? The absence of justice and clear thinking which robbed our man of his race is so enraging that it would be as well to pass on to something else. * * * * * And so we come to what ordinary laymen like you and me, who are not supposed to be able to interpret rules, might think to be a parallel, but which in "higher" circles passes unnoticed. At the "Kinnaird" Meeting D. Finlay, the English 120 yards hurdles champion, represented, quite rightly, Surrey Athletic Club. A WEEK later, at the British Games, in a programme of inter-club events, he competed for Milocarians A.C. in the short hurdles event. Later in the programme, he competed as a member of the Milocarian relay team—a team event, if ever there was one. These are the facts. Think them over! * * * * * Our contention is that the man in question would have been eligible to represent his new club in the hurdles (individual event) after three months' membership, but not in the relay (team event) until he had served twelve months' membership with his new club. * * * * * We are aware that we leave ourselves open to the cry "Two blacks don't make a white," but we contend that WE have yet to make a black mark! This business has its humorous side, for since the above events, Finlay has been entered as a member of a Surrey Athletic Club relay team! * * * * * Many of our members of ten years or so standing will remember B. C. Button, who in 1926 and 1927 showed great promise as a runner. He went to Australia with his parents, has had his share of racing successes, and now writes to say he is Hon. Secretary of the St. George District A.A.C. of New South Wales. He asks for news of former friends, and sends us the Annual Report of his club, which makes interesting reading. Their track standard seems to be quite a high one; but in the field events section there are some very fine performances. B. Dickinson has done 24 ft. 0 5-8 ins., Broad Jump, and 49 ft. 11 7-8 ins. Hop Step and Jump. Their best Shot Putt is 43 ft. 4in., Javelin Throw, 168ft. 5 ins.; Discus, 129 ft. 10½ ins Certainly, very good performances. It is good to know that one of our old comrades still enjoys good health, and is helping to carry on the sport in another part of the Empire. * * * * * It is indeed pleasing to see the introduction of so many boys to the Club recently. Among them are many who have distinguished themselves in school athletics; and we hope that in the course of a few years they will attain similar success in senior events. * * * * * At the British Games the "star" event was the Three Miles team race between Birchfield H. and ourselves; eight aside running, with six scoring. The race will be long remembered by those who had the pleasure to witness it. At one mile Birchfield led; at two miles we were leading handsomely, but in the last lap our Midland friends managed to pack in together and inflict a four points defeat upon us. Actually, the greatest excitement prevailed at the finish of the race, and he would have been a bold man who attempted to give the team winners without adding up the scoring positions. A four points deficit was our lot, but so close was the race that the gain of ten yards or so by one of our men on the last lap would probably have reversed the result. We congratulate Birchfield upon scoring one over us; and both teams were delighted with the match—and, may it be said, are eager for the next. Jim Ginty, of ours, led the field home in 14 min. 43 sec., and Ring and Rice did well to finish third and fourth. Final scores were Birchfield H. (2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9), 37 pts.; Belgrave H. (1, 3, 4, 10, 11, 12), 41 pts. Our scoring men were Ginty, Ring, Rice, Taylor, Allum, Parker; with Carter and D. Patience as the non-scoring men. * * * * * At the time of writing our two and three mile teams have competed in seven open team races and won five of them. Wins have been our reward at Luton, Chelmsford, St. Albans, Wealdstone and Ponders End. The least said about Ravensbourne the better! We were particularly pleased with our win at Ponders End, for our "B" team finished third—and Birchfield were second. Carter ran a fine race here, losing by inches to R. R. Sutherland, of Birchfield. Our success in these races is very gratifying, especially as we have had to do without the assistance of A. Penny, H. E. Footer and R. W. Jordan. * * * * * Recent individual winners of Open events include C. E. Churcher, F. R. Webb, A. R. Shaw, A. A. Bird, H. W. Shields, H. E. Footer, J. E. Flower (hush!), to whom our heartiest congratulations go. We were also winners of a scratch relay at Woking. * * * * * We had several representatives in the A.A.A. Championships, and D. E. Brown (2nd, 2 miles Walk), J. Ginty (2nd, 2 miles Steeplechase), T. H. Scrimshaw (4th, 880 yards), H. G. Churcher (5th, 2 miles Walk) and A. R. Shaw (Standard, Steeplechase) were our principal performers, and merit our sincere congratulations. Don Brown had to give place to Cooper in the Walk, but his time of 13 min. 53.8 sec. is amazingly fast. Tommy Scrimshaw ran splendidly (he was unofficially timed at 1 min. 55.4 secs.) and yet this only gained fourth place. Most years this time would carry a championship with it, but Tommy has always been unlucky in his running. We were all glad to see a good club-man in A. R. Shaw qualify for his Club Honours Badge; and Harry Churcher repeated a previous year's performance in gaining a Standard Medal. Of Jim Ginty we shall have something to say presently, but meanwhile,—well done, all! * * * * * It would be interesting to have a special trophy in connection with the A.A.A. Championships, to be held for a year by the club whose representatives scored most points, reckoning on a basis of six points for a winner, down to one point for the sixth man in a final, and a point for every man (not included in the foregoing) who beat standard for his event. Such a trophy would provide added interest to spectator and competitor alike, pay some tribute to clubs, who are, when all is said and done, the backbone and the life-blood of Athletics, and provide that little extra element of interest and keenness for the public. If such a scheme were instituted, it is interesting to note that on this year's results we should have been placed fourth—a very satisfying position to occupy. Scores would have been (E. & O.E., of course): Achilles 31, Polytechnic H. 26, L.A.C. 22, Belgrave 16, Melocarians 15, Woodford Green A.C. 12, Salford A.C. 12, Army A.A. 11. The sport at the A.A.A. Championship was tremendously keen, and everyone must have enjoyed Friday's and Saturday's programmes. But why, oh why, are we not allowed to know who has won Standard medals? We have complained about this before. There must be thousands of athletes in the crowd who appreciate what A.A.A. standard means. In a Club such as ours, the Honours Badge depends upon it, and yet competitor and spectator can get no information during the meeting. We suggest that out of courtesy to the competitors, and to that section of the spectators who are athletes enjoying a "busman's holiday," these details should be given immediately following the event. * * * * * All present on the Saturday were impressed by the performance of Ginty in the 2 miles Steeplechase, and his spirited running against George Bailey, of Salford, who eventually triumphed in very good time. Here, we thought, England has two of the finest steeplechasers she has ever been able to call upon. Reference to the records showed us that in the eighteen years that the times have been taken in this event, Jim's time (10 min. 29.8 sec.) had only been beaten twice, one occasion being when Iso Hollo, the Finnish world's record holder, had taken the title in 1933. Here, we thought, England has two men who will do well against France on July 27th, and against the rest of the world at Berlin in the 1936 Olympiad. But in some unaccountable way, despite the fact that the first two Englishmen were religiously chosen in all the other events for the match v. France, the second string in the Steeplechase was announced as "A. N. Other." We submit that the Selection Committee have allowed feelings other than strict impartiality, and attention to their own Championships, to influence them. It is pitiable that England should not have the services of one of the gamest triers and proved performers that have ever drawn on spikes. We are not unmindful of last year's selection of the team to visit Australia, when the claims of A. V. Reeve, of the Poly., were ignored. We trust that those in a position to do so will make enquiries into the matter, to ensure that such flagrant injustice shall not again be meted out to athletes who fully earn their selection; and consistently by their sportsmanship and whole-hearted endeavour, prove their worthiness to represent their country. We have sympathy for the man, game runner though he be, selected to take the place rightfully belonging to our man; for he is well aware that he is not the second-best steeplechaser in England, and, indeed, to the best of our knowledge, he has never yet competed in a Steeplechase event. Jim Ginty, sportsman that he is, refuses to discuss the matter; and we can only hope that the future will bring his International colours over both country and track, to compensate in some degree for present disappointments. STOP PRESS.—Subsequent events have shown that the Selection Committee robbed England of a probable three points, and at worst a certain one point, by their non-selection of Ginty. These points might have made all difference in such a closely-fought match. * * * * * Nearly sixty members and friends took part in the Club Outing on Sunday, July 21st. Our double-deck coach left Victoria at 10-15 a.m. and took us to Frensham Ponds, where the party swam, played cricket and rounders, and generally enjoyed themselves. It was good to see Arthur Penny lapping round the bases at full speed. A move was made to Elstead for tea, where the company tried, unsuccessfully, to demolish completely the home-made rolls, butter, jam, lashings of cream, and cake provided. After tea, we adjourned to Footer's idea of an open space (we suspect it was inside, for the pull-up was within a short distance of a hostelry!) and indulged in further games. Then, homewards. Everyone voted the day's outing a most successful one, and many enquired if another could not be arranged in a few weeks' time. The weather favoured us, and we were delighted to see some of our more recent members taking part in everything, and thoroughly enjoying themselves. items.sum: Juniors' report: Belgrave won all three events of a junior inter-club contest with Mitcham A.C. and Croydon H. at Mitcham on June 3rd, plus S. C. Botwright's Middlesex junior 220 yards title, H. M. Quackenbos's third in the A.A.A. junior steeplechase and a second place in an Enfield team race.
items.s: WITH THE JUNIORS. Juniors' report: Belgrave won all three events of a junior inter-club contest with Mitcham A.C. and Croydon H. at Mitcham on June 3rd, plus S. C. Botwright's Middlesex junior 220 yards title, H. M. Quackenbos's third in the A.A.A. junior steeplechase and a second place in an Enfield team race. On Monday, June 3rd, a Junior Inter-Club contest was held at Mitcham between the local club, Croydon H. and ourselves. We were successful in winning very convincingly the three events decided, and we congratulate ourselves upon having such splendid young runners in our ranks. We are sure that we shall be well represented in Senior events a few years hence, judging by the talent on show at this Inter-Club event, and in other races. It is not our policy to give our juniors too much racing, for we know the evils which such over-indulgence can inflict upon promising careers, but it is certainly very pleasing to see the Belgrave Harriers of to-morrow performing so creditably when called upon to represent the Club in junior fixtures. RESULTS. 3 x 100 Yards Relay.—1, Belgrave H. (Botwright, Jones, Saunders); 2, Mitcham A.C.; 3, Croydon H. 3 x 200 Yards Relay.—1, Belgrave H. (as above); 2, Mitcham A.C.; 3, Croydon H. 880 Yards Team Race.—1, Belgrave H. (Clements 2, Quackenbos 3; Cottrel, 5), 10 pts.; 2, Mitcham A.C. 11 pts. S. C. Botwright greatly distinguished himself by winning the Middlesex Junior 220 yards Championship; and he will undoubtedly show himself to be a first-class sprinter in a year or so; possibly developing into a champion quarter-miler. H. M. Quackenbos also merits our congratulations upon his third place in the A.A.A. Junior ¾-mile Steeplechase Championship. He will surely become one of our future stalwarts. Four of our young milers, Clements, Chantler, Stimpson and Wood competed in an under 20 mile team race at the Enfield A.C. Open Meeting, and although our scoring men finished 4, 5, 6, we were placed second. However, this form guarantees good future performances. Steady training, co-operative effort, willingness to learn and apply the principles expounded by the senior runners, and moderated racing during the early years, should develop within the Club a set of performers capable of bringing further lustre to the Club's name in the future. items.sum: Southern Amateur League Division 1 report: Belgrave fifth-placed team in the 4 x 220 yards relay at the White City on May 25th and winners of the 1 Mile Team race at Herne Hill on June 29th, leaving them one point behind Herne Hill and leaders Blackheath with two events left.
items.s: SOUTHERN AMATEUR LEAGUE EVENTS. Southern Amateur League Division 1 report: Belgrave fifth-placed team in the 4 x 220 yards relay at the White City on May 25th and winners of the 1 Mile Team race at Herne Hill on June 29th, leaving them one point behind Herne Hill and leaders Blackheath with two events left. Division 1. On May 25th, at the White City, was held the 4 x 220 yds. and we fielded a useful team in Kealey, Stroud, Mewes and Michael. Kealey elected to start for us, and drawing number 1 station, he was twice bumped very badly and so we lost any advantage which we might have had. Mewes and Michael both tried their best to reduce the gap between the leaders, and Stroud went off over the last leg just in front of the Poly and S.L.H. He could not hold Yates, of S.L.H., but just managed to beat Carmen, of the Poly, by inches for fifth position. Blackheath beat Herne Hill for first place, with Mitcham A.C. third. The 1 Mile Team race was held at Herne Hill on June 29th, and we repeated our last year's success in this race and all our men ran extremely well. Tom Scrimshaw, in finishing fourth in the actual race, which was won by the now A.A.A. champion, S. C. Wooderson, fully justified those who think he may do even better over longer distaces than he has done over the half. Our other three men, Bill Rice, Arthur Allum and Albert Shaw, finished 7, 8, 9, and so we scored 28 pts. to Blackheath H. 38, Mitcham A.C. 51, Poly H. 52, Herne Hill H. 59, and South London H. 72. Thus, with two events still to be decided, Blackheath are leading, with Herne Hill one point behind. We are one point behind them. So that with two points to make up, and the 1 Mile Medley Relay and the 4 x 880 yds. to take place, we can be fairly optimistic regarding our chances of retaining our title of champions. The big danger—and on their present form it is a very big one—are the present leaders, Blackheath Harriers. With S. C. Wooderson to lead them and men like Poole, Whittingham, Wiard, Parkes and Page, they present a very formidable opposition, and if our boys can pull it off, then they will have well deserved our congratulations. items.sum: Report of the Doris Shield inter-club contest at Battersea Park on June 26th, won back by Belgrave from holders Thames Valley Harriers by 28 points to 26 (Ashcombe A.C. 12), with the accompanying handicaps (100 yards, one mile, shot putt, 2 miles walk).
items.s: “DORIS” SHIELD INTER-CLUB CONTEST. Report of the Doris Shield inter-club contest at Battersea Park on June 26th, won back by Belgrave from holders Thames Valley Harriers by 28 points to 26 (Ashcombe A.C. 12), with the accompanying handicaps (100 yards, one mile, shot putt, 2 miles walk). This was held at Battersea Park Track on June 26th, and after an enjoyable evening's sport we managed to win back the Shield once again. The holders, Thames Valley Harriers, put up a stern fight, however, and we were only successful by the narrow margin of 2 points. In the 100 Yards match, Tavender, of T.V.H., just pipped Brodie in 10 2/5 secs., and with Stroud filling third place we managed to share points in this event. Points were scored on the basis of 6 to 1 in 100 to 440, and in the Team and Relay race they were 6—4—2. Tommy Scrimshaw turned out for us in the 440 Yards match event, and ran home an easy winner in 52 2/5 secs. T.V.H. men were second and third, with Michael fourth, and so once again points were even between the two clubs. By the way, Ashcombe A.C. were also competing but they had the last two men in both these races. In the 2 Miles Team race, Ashcombe did us a good turn by beating T.V.H. for second place in the team race. L. J. Cohen was the individual winner, with R. W. Jordan, who was making one of his rare appearances for us (he is now at Chichester, but happened to be on holiday, for which we were duly thankful), and he ran a fine race to finish second, with Tom Carter third. With Jack Flower fourth, we thus had an easy win, with, as mentioned above, Ashcombe finishing second and Thames Valley H. third. We now had a 4 points lead and, barring accidents, the Shield looked as good as won. For the final event, the 1 Mile Medley Relay, A. D. G. White, of T.V.H., gave his team a winning lead over the half-mile stage, and so we finished second with Ashcombe behind us. T.V.H. thus knocked two points off our lead, and the final scores were: Belgrave H. 28 pts., Thames Valley H. 26 pts., Ashcombe A.C. 12 pts. There were the usual handicaps open to each club, and in the 100 Yards we had all six finalists, and M. Holt scored his first win in club events; with S. C. Botwright, another of our promising Junior sprinters, second; and R. G. Michael third. The One Mile Handicap was won in rather easy fashion by G. V. Godfrey, of T.V.H., off the 155 mark, with C. E. Cheyney, now of Ashcombe, second and W. J. Ashford, of our own club, third. Our club also held a Shot Putt handicap with our new member from Germany, F. Grassau, on the scratch mark, but he failed to get placed, the winner being E. M. Waldron, with that consistent field event performer, S. Jones, second, and Eagle third. The 2 Miles Walk handicap resulted in a popular win for Jack Field, with J. Banfield, of Ashcombe, second and W. Snell, of our club, third. items.s: INTER-CLUB RELAY MEETING AT CROYDON. Report of the inter-club relay meeting on Croydon's ground on July 2nd (4 x 100, 4 x 880, 4 x 300 yards and 1 mile team race), after which Mitcham and Belgrave led the Shield contest with 25 points each. This was held on July 2nd on Croydon's ground, which is quite close to the Croydon Aerodrome, and the track has a nasty gradient which has to be "climbed" five times in the course of a mile race. However, the 4 x 100 opened the proceedings and, as usual, we filled our usual third position with Croydon beating Mitcham for first place. In the 4 x 880 yds. we fielded a useful team, and with Frank Webb giving us the lead over the second stage, and Alec Ball keeping it, Tommy Scrimshaw just "sauntered" round for the last leg. In fact he almost went too slow and gave the rest of us a few hearts attacks when Ayton, of Mitcham, got to his shoulder at the last bend. Tommy, however, with a quick glance round, immediately sprinted away from him, and we realised Tom had been gently pulling our legs. The 4 x 300 yds. was a repetition of last year's race, in that it caused tremendous excitement, and although Croydon had a winning lead over the last leg, Tom Scrimshaw chased the Mitcham boy all the way and although he caught him, on the narrow track he could not quite get by, and they finished with Tom and his opponent "locked" together as they flashed past the post. The verdict of the Judges was: Croydon, Mitcham, Belgrave and Epsom, and so once again we just failed by the proverbial inch. In the 1 Mile Team race our men, ably led by our Captain, Bill Rice, kept together in fine style at the head of the field, and although on the last lap Frost, of Croydon, went into the lead with 300 yards and go, Harry Shields raced away and finished in easy winner in time which was very good considering the state of the track. Our men scored 1, 2, 4, 6, and in spite of our Captain trying to "wangle" things, Mitcham beat Croydon by 2 points for second place. When we totalled the scores, we found that the home club, Mitcham and ourselves each scored 12 points on the evening, and so Mitcham and Belgrave still lead with 25 points each, with Croydon 21, and Epsom 9.
