items.s: SOCIAL. Social notes on the first dance and social of the 1935–36 season and the list of coming socials and dances, with applications to W. L. Bayliss. Our first Dance and first Social of the season have already been held. Our Dance was held at the Express Rooms, Clapham Junction, on September 14th, and was very successful. The Social at Wimbledon, on October 5th, was well-attended; and the fun fast and furious. Social and Dance dates are given below, and we look to every member to help the social programme along, and do his best to support the functions arranged. Nov. 2nd—SOCIAL, at Wimbledon. Nov. 23rd—DANCE, at Express Rooms, Clapham Junction. Dec. 14th—SOCIAL, at Wimbledon. Dec. 31st—CARNIVAL DANCE, at Queensberry Hall, South Kensington. Jan 25th, 1936—SOCIAL, at Wimbledon. The usual 5 miles Handicap which brings the realities of another busy imminent Winter season home to us, was held on October 5th; and attracted a fine entry of 26. Dick Northover was first away, followed 45 seconds later by Don Heath, and then came the others with varying allowances, until Don Brown left the post of honour. As last year, Harry Churcher again showed that he requires practically no preparation (unlike most of us who have to train for months to achieve something like fitness!) and won fairly easily, recording fastest time in doing so. Colin Sutton won his first prize with us during his three years of membership; and now that he has settled down to training again he should claim his place in our "Junior" team. Jack Rutland took third place and continues to improve. Len Fletcher was noticed moving in something like his old style; and two newcomers in S. R. Wood and W. C. items.label: November 1935
items.sum: T. Cotton's Building Fund notes on unreturned Belgrave Building Bricks, pinboards, the Supporters' Club and the new Building Fund Sub-Committee, with a holiday anecdote about the Hon. Editor and the Editor's bracketed reply.
items.s: BUILDING FUND NEWS. T. Cotton's Building Fund notes on unreturned Belgrave Building Bricks, pinboards, the Supporters' Club and the new Building Fund Sub-Committee, with a holiday anecdote about the Hon. Editor and the Editor's bracketed reply. By T. Cotton. There is one thing puzzling me greatly just at present, and that is where do Belgrave Building Bricks go after being issued? Since September, 1934, we have handed bricks out in plenty, and were inclined to pat ourselves on the back, until we found the discrepancy between exports and imports. Sometimes, very rarely, our young lives have been made joyous by a box suddenly finding its way back. This, as I have already said, very rarely. We can only draw mental pictures of bright yellow boxes used to support aspidasras, or gold-fish bowls; and are considering having some done in pink, or light blue, for the more dainty type of member. Really, we should be hearing more about these bricks. The Supporters' Club scheme is a great success, but one feels that the original plan of the "Building Fund" was so sound that it is disappointing to note the poor efforts made with these bricks. Concerning pinboards, I shall welcome payment for all those completed. We still have a few of the larger boards on hand. Please note that no member can secure more than one "600" board at a time. As everybody seems to know, our Supporters' Club is a great success. Some of the figures I have heard regarding profits have been amazing (especially to Frank Elson and myself, who are responsible for the scheme), but to be candid, we are very delighted with the support given. There are some ways in which you can help Frank and myself a great deal. You know by now that one or other of us is always present on Tuesday and Thursday evenings at "The Rising Sun"; at Wimbledon on Saturdays; and at Battersea Park on Sunday mornings. Please try and square all accounts as quickly as possible, so that we can complete our accounts speedily. Then there is another important point being neglected by some. It is essential that we have the name and address of every member of the Supporters' Club on our books. If you have any outstanding names and addresses, please let me have them immediately. To be of full value, these details should be legible. One hopes after the fine efforts made by all just recently, and with the day when we really can make a move drawing nearer, that many will remain to enjoy the advantages of our our headquarters. I cannot help thinking that a bachelor really does perhaps get more out of such things and I must give warning to my friend the Editor. During our holidays I exerted every possible effort to keep him from the wiles and trickery of women. On board the boat going over I did have a spot of bother over one lady who was greatly impressed by his method of leaning over the rail when sea-sick, but it passed. For two whole weeks did I exert all my known good (?) influence, and many the good talking-to I gave him. Then, gentle reader, then when we have returned with unblemished reputations, I stroll into the "Swan" on the night of our first Social, and behold a sight that tears my heart with pain. The Hon. Editor, plus cigarette and beer, standing by the piano, crooning! Oh, Alfred! beware! [Editorial Interpolation.—Seeing that the above comes from the pen of our old friend, Tom Cotton, it is hardly necessary for me to make reply. You all know what his remarks are worth. (Thank you, Bert!) But what base ingratitude this youngster shows to one who has taken him by the hand for the past five years; and safely seen him through his holidays! Were I given to washing dirty Cotton linen (something wrong here!) in public; never again would waters run clear and undefiled. And so, I refrain, conscious of the old adage, " . . . . where angels fear to tread"] A new "Building Fund" Sub-Committee has been elected and consists of A. E. Taylor, A. A. Harley (the same), H. Parker, E. Gordon, F. H. Elson and yours truly; and, of course, the President, Gen. Hon. Secretary and Hon. Treasurer, ex officio. Frank and I have been specially placed on this Sub-Committee because of our known ability for being cursed by people who cannot obtain sufficient membership cards. So don't mind us, carry on cursing! items.s: IMPORTANT ! Notice of the subscription increase approved at the Special General Meeting of 31 October 1935, including four free issues of the Belgravian, with a request to pay arrears and for Gazette Fund donations. At the Special General Meeting held at "The Rising Sun" on October 31st, after discussion, the proposal of the Committee to increase subscriptions to 8/- per annum for Senior members; 4/- per annum for Junior members (under 18); and 1/- per annum for Boys (under 15); was approved, and becomes operative immediately. This subscription is to include the free distribution of four issues of the "Belgravian" annually, and there is no doubt that our subscription value is still the greatest obtainable among athletic clubs. Arising from the above, all members are asked to settle their liabilities for past "Belgravians" immediately, and so enable the books to be closed. A considerable amount is outstanding and prompt settlement would be appreciated. As hitherto, any donations to the "Gazette Fund" will be gratefully accepted and acknowledged, and should be sent to the Hon. Editors, or to the Hon. Treasurer. Addresses appear on page 1. The Rising Sun

items.label: February 1936
items.h:
THE XIth OLYMPIAD.
Berlin, August 1st to 16th.
items.sum: Preview of the 1936 Berlin Olympic Games describing the flame relay and the Reich Sport Field venues, recalling that Britain's only two winners at Los Angeles in 1932 were Belgrave Harriers.
items.s: THE XIth OLYMPIAD. Berlin, August 1st to 16th. Preview of the 1936 Berlin Olympic Games describing the flame relay and the Reich Sport Field venues, recalling that Britain's only two winners at Los Angeles in 1932 were Belgrave Harriers. Many of our members' thoughts are turning towards the Olympic Games. Some hope to carry the British vest on to track or road, some to attend as spectators, while the great majority will have to be content with the newspaper reports; but all will be interested to know of the preparations being made to receive the World's athletes. Since the Games were revived at Athens in 1896 they have been held in different countries at regular intervals of four years. Berlin will act as host in 1936, and countless thousands will take advantage of the opportunity to pay a visit to the German capital. On the opening day the teams of more than fifty nations will march into the Stadium with their national flags and take the Olympic oath of true comradeship. A great relay of runners will carry the sacred fire from the ancient scene of the games at Olympia in Greece to Berlin, where the Olympic Flame on the tower of the Stadium will be lit while a salute of honour thunders forth. The great white flag with the five linked rings, symbolizing the five continents, will be hoisted on the mast of the arena before the eyes of a hundred thousand spectators. The Olympic Bell will be heard for the first time, summoning, as it is intended to do, "the youth of the world," and then the world championships in more than nineteen forms of sport will be carried out in the course of two weeks. We are, of course, particularly interested in the Athletics part of the programme, and this will extend from August 2nd to August 9th. The track will be at Grunewald, one of the western suburbs of Berlin, and is rapidly nearing completion. Here on the former Race Course, in an area of 262 acres (about three-quarters of the space occupied by Hyde Park) 2,500 men are at work constructing one of the most magnificent sports grounds in the world. Twenty minutes' journey from the centre of Berlin brings one to the South Gate of the Reich's Sport Field. Entering the Field one is immediately confronted with the huge concrete-built Olympic Stadium. This has an outside elevation of 48 feet, while the arena itself is sunk 42 feet below the surface. There is accommodation for 100,000 spectators, most of whom can be seated on its 30 miles of seats. The South side of the Stadium is occupied by the tribune of honour, where the distinguished guests will be seated. At the western curve is an entrance for competitors, and at the eastern end lies the main gate, above which the Olympic Torch will burn throughout the Games. Two tunnel entrances in the west curve lead to the dressing rooms which are under the grandstands. The athletic contests will be staged here, and also the finals of the football, handball and equestrian events. The arena consists of a football field surrounded by a 400-metre track. In the semi-circular spaces between the ends of the football field and the curves of the track are javelin grounds, spaces for high jump and putting the shot, as well as arenas for the discus and hammer events. Outside the 30 feet wide track, down either "straight," are the grounds for the pole vault, the long jump, and the hop, step and jump. Many visitors to the stadium have commented on the excellence of the turf on the infield. The secret is that it has been laid with ten-year-old turf taken from a neighbouring field. North of the Olympic Stadium lies the Swimming and Diving Stadium, with room for 18,000 spectators. The diving and swimming pools are separated by a concrete wall so that it will be possible to hold both diving and swimming contests at the same time. A heating plant has been installed in order that the water may be kept at an even temperature. The International Swimming Association requires that this shall be 70 degrees Fahrenheit. A few inches below the level of the water a curved gutter has been built into the walls of the pool. This will break the waves caused by the swimmers, so that the water will always be comparatively calm. To the East of the Swimming Stadium lie practice grounds, tennis courts, the hockey stadium, and basket ball grounds. The women competitors will live in the Sports Forum during the Games. The men will be housed in the Olympic Village which is being built at Döberitz, nine miles away along the main Hamburg road. Immediately to the west of the main Stadium lies the Assembly Ground, presided over by the 220 feet high Führer Tower. From this Tower will peal forth the Olympic Bell to announce the opening of the Games on August 1st, 1936. A single peal of the bell will also precede the announcement of each result. The Assembly Ground will be used for Polo contests. South of this, occupying the extreme south-west corner of the Sports Field, in a delightful sylvan setting, lies the equestrian stadium. In the north-west corner of the Field is the Dietrich Eckart Open Air Theatre. Here in a vast semi-circular natural arena, surrounded by woodland, the largest open-air theatre in the world has been built. It will seat 20,000 people. The gymnastic contests will be held here and a number of dramatic performances will be given during the Games. The Festival Play to be presented on the evening of the opening day of the Games will, however, be staged in the Olympic Stadium itself. We are, of course, very hopeful that we shall have several members in the British team. It is with pleasure that we recall that Britain's only two winners at Los Angeles in 1932 were both Belgrave Harriers, and that both had carried our colours with distinction prior to their trip across the Atlantic. We trust that the shorter journey to Berlin will provide other Belgrave Harriers with their chance to emulate their club-mates of four years ago. And so, best of luck! Olympic Games Berlin Athens Olympia Grunewald Hyde Park Döberitz Los Angeles Belgrave Harriers

e: South of the Thames Cross-country Championship
items.s: THIS AND THAT. Club notes: subscriptions, members' news (Bill Rice, A. O. Tookey, the Patience brothers in Egypt, new members Verney, Goodale and Kemp), Olympic possibles, a new club tie, early-season cross-country matches and coming fixtures. This is the second issue of our Gazette to be issued quarterly under the new arrangements passed by the Club at the Special General Meeting held on October 31st, 1935. Every member should automatically receive his copy, and members are requested to notify any change of address promptly. It is also pointed out, once again, that this is your Gazette. Your suggestions and contributions are wanted. Team work is a very necessary part in the production of a journal such as this, and you are asked to do your bit Please write to the Hon. Editor saying what you like about the "Belgravian," where you think improvements can be effected, and pass on any bright ideas likely to interest, help or amuse your fellow-members. Thank you! * * * * * Your Hon. Treasurer would be glad to receive outstanding subscriptions (8/- Senior, 4/- Juniors, 1/- Boys) which became due in September. The business of spending the Club's money is quite arduous enough, without reluctant members causing extra work in the collection of subscriptions. Members who have an account outstanding against their names in respect of "Belgravians" received up to our last issue, are asked to send this amount on to the Hon. Editors. It is desired to close this matter as soon as possible, and your co-operation would be welcomed. * * * * * Bill Rice continues to show slow progress, but we are glad to know that his health is improving, even though it will probably be many weeks before he is back to normal. His interest in Club affairs is as keen as ever, although he is unable to come along and enjoy our jokes and take his part in our Club affairs. When he does so, we can all assure him of a very hearty welcome. * * * * * Congratulations and best wishes to A. O. Tookey, who has recently joined the married ranks. * * * * * In October we bade Dan Patience and brother Rod au revoir, when they left England for Egypt, where they will be stationed for some time. Both had endeared themselves to us by their modest bearing and enthusiasm for the Club. We expect to have them out with us again when they return to England. Meanwhile, news comes from Egypt that Dan has recently won the Egyptian Command Championship, upon which we most heartily congratulate him. An old friend in Cotterell was second. * * * * * Writing of Dan Patience reminds us of his splendid running in last year's "Southern," when he had to stop in the early stages to adjust a shoe, losing dozens of places, and yet ran brilliantly to score in our team. Since this race, one of the members of the winning team has been declared ineligible, and so Surrey A.C.'s margin over us was reduced to a bare point. It is as well, perhaps, that we were not made winners of the Championship by this adjustment. We would much rather regain it on our merits this year, although we do not minimise the strength of the opposition. * * * * * The Southern Cross-country Championships are to be held from Sandown Racecourse on February 22nd. Both Junior and Senior events will be decided, and the nearness of the venue should enable many of our members to attend and help our men on. * * * * * We are glad to know that Harry Verney's application to be considered a first-claim member of our Club without serving the usual qualifying period, has been acceded to by the special committee appointed to consider such cases. Verney, a former Civil Service Cross-country champion and Birchfield Harrier, has shown that he has real ability, and we wish him luck in his quest for a place in our championship teams. The A.A.A. 10 miles running and 7 miles walking championships are to be held at the White City on April 11th—during the Easter holiday. No doubt we shall be well represented and it is whispered that Arthur Penny has his eyes on the 10 miles title. * * * * * Our readers are requested to note that the date of the London—Brighton Relay has been altered. It is now intended to hold this event (probably starting from Mitcham) on April 25th. Please note your fixture list accordingly. It will probably be necessary to alter the date of our 5 miles road handicap in view of this change. * * * * * The A.A.A. have recently circularised about 150 athletes, advising them that they are under consideration for Olympic selection, and urging them to take particular care in their preparation. Final selection will be made after the A.A.A. Championships (July 10th and 11th) and, of course, it is quite likely that there will be some "turn-ups'" when the team is finally selected. Our members to receive the official letter are: J. E. Flower (10,000 metres), J. Ginty (Steeplechase), J. Parker (5,000 and 10,000 metres), A. W. Penny (5,000 and 10,000 metres), G. H. Powell (Javelin), and T. H. Scrimshaw (800 metres). No walkers have been advised, but here the A.A.A. are acting in concert with the R.W.A., and there is little doubt that several of our men are on the "probables" list. Good luck to all our athletes in their quest for Olympic honours; those named above, and others! * * * * * The Committee have decided to order a newly-designed tie for the use of members. This tie will have the inner portion of the Club badge (portcullis and cross keys) woven in gold on a dark red background; and will supersede the present striped pattern. Many members have suffered the embarrassment, when wearing the old pattern tie, of being asked if they are an "Old Reptillian," etc., and we do not doubt that many South London Harriers have been surprised (albeit flattered) when claimed as a Belgrave Harrier by those whose colour values are not their strong point. The new design should obviate all this, and should, in addition, by reason of its better toning with the ordinary lounge suit, prove very popular and be much in evidence at Club functions and elsewhere. This tie will sell at 3/- each and be obtainable from our Hon. Treasurer, so advise him of your requirements at once. Some of the well-known rugby clubs have adopted such badge-woven ties which are sold at 6/6 to 8/6 each, but, as far as is known, we shall be the first athletic club to favour this new development in sports ties. Among others we have welcomed to the Club recently are T. F. Goodale and J. W. Kemp. The latter has shown up prominently in Bank races, has been third in the Southern Junior Cross-country Championship, and generally given evidence that he will be an asset to our teams in due course. Goodale was third in the Southern Counties 880 yards Championship last season, and won the Army Championship at this distance. He has well-beaten two minutes for the distance on several occasions, and as he expects to settle down in the South before long, he, too, should add to our strength. * * * * * Congratulations to our team in the Surrey County Cross-country championship on holding their title. Also to Arthur Penny on his success in the Surrey race; to Pat Parker upon winning the Sussex title; and to E. Simpson upon winning the Middlesex Junior Championship and so following in the footsteps of Harry Shields, with, of course, something to spare. * * * * * One of our early races of the season was versus University of London A.C., at Coulsdon. We had a very easy win (98 points to 202), supplying the first seven men to finish. Parker, Penny and Cohen finished equal first, closely followed by Shaw, Williams and Verney. We were obviously much too strong for our University friends, who lacked the assistance of Etheridge; but, nevertheless, the sporting match was greatly enjoyed by all. * * * * * On the same day the remainder of our forces met Thames Valley Harriers over their Cranford course, and in a very exciting race we managed to win by four points (148 to 152, scoring 12 aside). Arthur Allum, followed by George Chantler, led the field home. * * * * * Our encounter with Metropolitan Police A.C. at Imber Court on November 16th showed us in a very heartless mood, for we had no fewer than the first fourteen home! Then came W. D. Symes, for the Police (he is also a member of our Club); and final scores, twenty aside, were 220 points to 716 points by the Police. Pat Parker was the actual winner of the race. A visit to Imber Court is always most enjoyable, and many of our runners and walkers (the walk is described elsewhere) remained to tea, and for the dancing which followed. * * * * * Track fixtures are at the moment the concern of the appropriate sub-committee; and they are busily planning our summer season. We have been able to book six Wednesday dates at Battersea Park for our evening meetings, and two Saturday afternoons, but we are not yet sure of a Saturday fixture in May, with which we usually open the season. * * * * * Our Championship Day has been arranged for July 25th. This is a week earlier than usual, and has been so arranged to allow those of our members who intend visiting the Olympic Games, either as competitors or spectators, to do so without missing the Club Championships. * * * * * A final word. The Championship season is fast approaching. "South of the Thames Senior," "Southern," "Junior" Walk "National" (English Championship, strictly), and "Senior" Walk follow one another rapidly. See that you do your little bit to help our teams along. Buy a new tie, and a packet of throat lozenges, and help things along! Bill Rice Bill Rice recovering slowly from ill health A. O. Tookey A. items.s: THE HIGHGATE HARRIERS' OPEN WALK. Report and result of the Highgate Harriers' open walk (short of seven miles), won by A. A. Cooper, in which Belgrave won the team race with 19 points and regained the Berman Cup (as printed, T. W. Green's handicap time does not match his time less allowance, and the placings 3, 4, 5 and 8 add to 20, not 19). The first Open event of the season was promoted by the Highgate Harriers on the last Saturday in October. It was necessary to find a different course from that generally used, owing to road-work, and it would appear that the course chosen was well short of the advertised seven miles. From the start our men were prominent, and at the half-way mark Harry Churcher led the field. He was forced to yield to Cooper and Stone before the end was reached, but this effort of Harry's must rank as one of his best. Tommy Green, young as ever, and Len Fletcher, who we were all glad to see on the road once again, and Bill Treacher, completed our team. Our score was the very low one of 19 points; and second came Surrey Walking Club, with 73 points. This win brought the "Berman Cup" back to our possession. The form of our men was quite encouraging and we left the first race of the season, feeling confident of more successes to come. Handicap awards eluded us, but Bill Snell won a special prize for the fastest handicap time from the Club providing the largest entry. Pos. Name Act. Time Allce. H'cap Time 1 A. A. Readman walked splendidly in his first Open race and promises to do well in the future; and the walking of our men generally gave great satisfaction. 103 finished. Pos. Name Act. Time Allce. items.label: February 1936
items.sum: Report of Belgrave's sixteenth open 7 miles walk at Wimbledon, where Woodford Green A.C. narrowly won the scratch team race and Percy Wright took the first handicap prize.
items.s: OUR OPEN WALK. Report of Belgrave's sixteenth open 7 miles walk at Wimbledon, where Woodford Green A.C. narrowly won the scratch team race and Percy Wright took the first handicap prize. Our open 7 miles event—the sixteenth we have promoted—took place at Wimbledon on the last Saturday in November, as usual. Compared with other entries this season, ours was the best received, but, unfortunately, there were 31 fewer than last year. One hundred and fifty-eight names came in this year (19 teams) and these figures condemned us to a financial loss, despite the very generous support given by several friends. Athletically, the event was the usual success, and our race with its by no means easy course seems to exercise a hold over the ordinary walker, which makes him come along year by year to see if he really can get up those hills without undue distress! This year we saw one of the finest tussles ever for scratch team honours. The teams concerned were Woodford Green A.C. and ourselves. Up to the half-distance the advantage was ours, but shortly afterwards Green, in attempting to race Cooper, was ruled out. This levelled matters, and the team fight was on. Eventually, victory went to our Woodford friends. We finished our fourth man before theirs, but Woodford's 1 and 3 points for their first two men home gave them the advantage and a few points win. Well done, Woodford Green! Meanwhile, Percy Wright, of our D team, was doing splendidly and with 19th position and 7 mins. 10 secs allowance, claimed the first handicap prize. Well walked, Percy! Our "D" team (Wright, Readman, Goold and Earle) took the first handicap team prizes, and so we can consider we had our share. Other awards appear below. Len Fletcher took the prize for the first Belgrave Harrier not gaining any other award, and a special prize (presented by Mr. W. Allen) for the first man in the scratch race with an allowance of 7 mins. or over, and not gaining any other award, went to R. A. Staker, of Highgate Harriers. We were particularly pleased to welcome teams from Dunlop W.C. and Leicester W.C., from the provinces; but they were unable to record any successes. Our own Club entry was very good and four teams were entered. In concluding, we should like to record our very sincere appreciation of the help given us by R.W.A. officials and others, and offer our thanks to the competitors who entered our race. We are also especially grateful to Messrs. Askew, Bayliss, Elson, Gordon and Thomson for their support of the Prize Fund, and to Mr. W. Allen for presenting a special prize. 129 finished. P. G. e: Belgrave Harriers v Metropolitan Police Walking Club
items.s: AT IMBER COURT. Report and result of the seven miles walking match against the Metropolitan Police Walking Club at Imber Court on November 16th, which ended in a dead-heat at 134 points each. On November 16th we met the Metropolitan Police Walking Club, at Imber Court, over their usual seven miles course. We were without the two Churchers and one or two other stalwarts, but our team looked good enough to win. From the command to start, Len Fletcher and Don Brown took the lead, which they gradually increased throughout, without ever distressing themselves. Places were changing continually among the rest of the field, and eventually we finished six men in the first eight home—and yet the complete team result proved a dead-heat! The reason for this was the splendid packing of our Police friends in the middle portion of the field—a factor which has led to our defeat in the past. Among those who enabled the Police to level-up the advantage gained by our earlier men were noticed several Police walkers who are also Belgrave men. Full details appear below. Pos. items.s: THE 7 MILES "JUNIOR" WALK. Report of the club 7 miles "Junior" walk for the "Horwood" Cup, won by C. E. Churcher from the holder C. Speechley, with "Doug" Earle taking the sealed handicap. Competition to hold the "Horwood" Cup was expected to be very keen, and 14 competitors lined up to take their chance in championship and handicap. A terrific struggle was expected between the holder, C. Speechley and our Captain, C. E. Churcher. This was forthcoming from the first few yards. Charlie, the elder, tried his hardest to get away on the hills, but Charlie, the younger, had a very slight advantage on the flat—and this advantage enabled him to show slighty more speed over the finish, and to win by seven seconds. This reversed the result of last year's race, when Speechley gained a very narrow victory over Churcher. P. G. Wright again showed improved form and the time he recorded was very creditable. He will certainly strengthen our "Junior" team. Rutland can do better than the time he recorded on this occasion. The fifth man, "Doug" Earle, with a 5-min. allowance, carried off the sealed handicap, with Frank Jarvis, who followed him in, and with the same allowance, second. There were a few absentees from this race, which is, of course, confined to those members possessing the R.W.A. "Junior" qualification; and it would have been interesting to see how Storey, R. F. Elson, Brian, Readman, Goold and Boddington (to mention a few) would have fared, had it been possible for them to turn out. Pos. Name Act. Time H'cap H'cap Time H'cap Pos. 1 C. E. items.label: February 1936
items.sum: Walking notes on the season so far, the "Berman" Cup and its past winners, prospects for the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship at Hendon, the fog-bound race v. Surrey W.C., the Croydon to Godstone race and coming fixtures.
e: Croydon to Godstone and Back Walk
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes on the season so far, the "Berman" Cup and its past winners, prospects for the R.W.A. "Junior" Championship at Hendon, the fog-bound race v. Surrey W.C., the Croydon to Godstone race and coming fixtures. The season has opened well for us, with scratch team wins in the Highgate and Enfield events, and a narrow and honourable defeat at the hands of Woodford Green A.C. in our own promotion. Gratifying as it is to meet with success in such events, it is in the championships that we hope to demonstrate supremacy over other clubs, and to add the Belgrave name to the Championship trophies once again, in the year 1936—the year when a Belgrave Harrier holds office as President of the Road Walking Association. * * * * * Our team win in the Highgate Harriers Open race carried with it the "Berman" Cup, which is annually competed for in connection with 7 mile events, and may be won outright by three successive wins. This is the fourth occasion on which we have been successful. Previous winners are as follows : 1927, Surrey A.C.; 1928, Belgrave H.; 1929, Herne Hill Harriers; 1930, Belgrave H.; 1931, Enfield A.C.; 1932, Enfield A.C.; 1933, Belgrave H.; 1934, Surrey Walking Club; 1935, Belgrave H. * * * * * The R.W.A. "Junior" Championship is to be held on March 7th, from the Police quarters at Hendon. A give-and-take course has been planned and arrangements are well in hand. It is only necessary for our prospective team to train hard and conscientiously for success to be our lot in this event. We have talent available good enough to take the gold medals and "Garnet" Cup, and it is only a matter of those with the ability doing the very necessary strolling and training spins for their efforts to be crowned with success. A Belgrave win is due. Our last was in 1933 (Birmingham : H. G. Churcher, D. E. Brown, A. H. Field, A. A. Harley), the one before that in 1930 (Enfield : F. H. Elson, E. Saunders, J. E. Field, S. L. King). Three years elapsed between these two wins, and now we are in the third season since our last victory. So get to it, Belgrave Juniors! Shall we be able to write : 1936, Belgrave H. (Hendon : ———, ———, ———, ———)? Our chances are undoubtedly bright. A third successive win by Surrey W.C. is most unlikely. Chief contenders should be Dunlop W.C., Sutton Coldfield W.C., London Vidarians W.C., and ourselves. We can do it; and I hope every member who can do so will come to Hendon on March 7th, and encourage our team. Last year Surrey W.C. equalled our record of four wins in this event. It's time to draw away again! * * * * * Writing of championships reminds me that the "Senior" 20 miles Championship is to be held at Leicester on May 9th, and the 50 kilos Championship, of which we are holders, at Derby on July 4th. This race will be of particular importance this year, in view of the Olympic race at this distance. * * * * * In addition to the events, results of which are given elsewhere, we have had a race versus Surrey W.C. over their Croydon to West Wickham and back course. At least, it can hardly be termed a race, for, owing to dense fog, our numbers were very small. For some time a race at all was very doubtful, then a shortened course was discussed, but finally it was decided to carry through with the event. Charlie Churcher walked splendidly to win the race, covering the 9¾ miles in 1 hour 20 mins. 51 secs. Jack Bidgood was 8th, Wright 10th, Saunders 14th, and Frank Elson 19th. Chief recollections are of terrible conditions, and of some fine walking by Churcher in spite of the fogginess. And ironically enough, after the race had finished, the fog lifted! * * * * * On Boxing Day, a weak team represented the Club in the Croydon to Godstone and back race (18¾ miles); and took third place to two teams from the promoting club. Our walkers finished as follows: 12th A. A. Harley (2 hr. 53 min. 35 sec); 14th, J. E. Field (2 hr. 56 min. 47 sec.); 15th, P. G. Wright (3 hr. 0 min. 24 sec.); 18th, W. H. Snell (3hr. 1 min. 4 sec.). Jack Field was placed fourth in the handicap, the actual winner of the scratch race, H. A. Hake, taking third prize. * * * * * On February 1st we shall support the London Transport Open 7 miles race at Bellingham; and on February 15th, the Ashcombe A.C. 10 miles Walk from Sheen. This latter event is not shown in our fixture list. On February 8th, the Saturday falling between the above-mentioned dates, the Valentines S.C. promote a 10 miles race from their quarters at Chadwell Heath. We have yet to decide whether it will be possible to support this event, in view of the large amount of racing to be done at this time of the year. March 7th is, of course, "Junior" day, as mentioned above, followed by the County Championships a fortnight later, and the Inter-county race on March 28th. Our Club 20 miles Championship is fixed for April 18th, and by this time all our distance men will be intent on gaining the Senior Championship for the Club. Last year we lost by one point, the previous year by two points. This year should give us compensation for these narrow disappointments, but come what may, our walkers may be depended upon to put up a good show and maintain the Belgrave reputation in this event, which includes four wins and six placings in the fifteen post-war years. items.label: February 1936
items.sum: Report and Belgrave result of the South of Thames "Junior" cross-country team race at Epsom Downs on November 9th, won individually by E. H. M. Williams, with Belgrave third in the team race; the result prints 38th before 28th.
items.s: THE SOUTH OF THAMES "JUNIOR" RACE. Report and Belgrave result of the South of Thames "Junior" cross-country team race at Epsom Downs on November 9th, won individually by E. H. M. Williams, with Belgrave third in the team race; the result prints 38th before 28th. The South of Thames "Junior" team race was held at Epsom Downs on November 9th, the weather being ideal for running, and we looked forward to a good race. E. H. M. Williams, of our club, proved an easy winner of the individual race. He led throughout, and after being with Hengle, of the Police, at half-way, came away from his field to win comfortably. E. G. Saunders ran finely to finish 10th, coming through strongly over the last mile; and K. N. Wood also did well in being 28th. Then came what was for us an unfortunate happening. J. W. Chamberlain in his first open race, finished 38th, an excellent performance, but was running for our "B" team, and so of course could not count for our "A" team. We thus had to go back to 60th for our fourth man, J. C. Edwards, and so finished third in the team race with 99 points. Reading A.C. "A" team secured first place with 50 pts., and the Metropolitan Police A.C. were second with 97 pts. It will be seen that with Chamberlain counting we should have been an easy second, but these little upsets are always liable in races of this description. Of the other members who ran for us, A. H. e: Belgrave Harriers v Ashcombe A.C. v Ealing Harriers
items.s: FIVE MILES HANDICAP. Report and result of the club five miles sealed handicap on November 23rd, run with a match against Ashcombe A.C. and Ealing Harriers which Belgrave won with 39 points; D. Martin won the handicap. On November 23rd we telescoped two events into one, viz., a Club five miles sealed handicap, and a match versus Ashcombe A.C. and Ealing Harriers. For the match event we nominated a team, as we had no desire to overwhelm our friends with our large numbers in a six aside to score match. Edwards, of Ealing, was placed first in the match, followed by Martin, of ours, Shirley (of Ashcombe) and then Stimpson and Chantler, of ours. We ran out winners with 39 points, to Ealing's 54, and Ashcombe's 78. In "our" race, Parker and Penny finished together, as the appended result shows. The handicap was almost a complete triumph for our "under 21" brigade. D. Martin took first place, with Stimpson second, and Merryman third (dead-heat). Frank Webb, snaky as ever, managed to spoil our juniors' exclusiveness by dead-heating for third place. Fifth (paired with F. A. Walker) came veteran George Still, well over the half-century, and still with plenty of energy, and a remarkable example of economy of effort in running to our youngsters. Twenty-four men finished within 73 seconds of the winner in the handicap, which was not too bad in an attempt to satisfy everyone! A glance at the attached result will show that we had a good entry and close racing. † Dead Heat. Pos. Name Act. Time H'cap H'cap Time H'cap Pos. 1 J. Parker 29 23 0 5 29 18 30 1 A. e: Belgrave Harriers Seven Miles Cross-Country Championship
items.s: THE SEVEN MILES CHAMPIONSHIP. C. T. Carter's account of the club seven miles cross-country championship, led by "Nutty" Penny, with the full result (A. W. Penny first, K. N. Wood first on handicap) and Belgrave Harriers beating Cadogan A.C. 52-84 on varsity scoring; the result prints "23†" for D. W. Martin's handicap position although no one shares his handicap time. In being given the honour of writing the account of our seven miles cross-country championship, I can only plead that I would rather have been running, if only to pass the honour on to a competent writer. Unfortunately, the absence of Pat Parker and Jim Ginty and one or two others robbed the race of some of its interest. The start, I thought, was rather a fast one, with "Nutty" Penny leading the way. After seeing the runners across to the Golf Course, I made my way to the Windmill. Here Penny was leading Les Cohen by 39 secs., with Allum a further 20 secs. behind in third place. Williams, Taylor, Ring, Shields and Flower followed. Then came a batch of runners, led by our Captain, H.E.F. On reaching the Windmill the second time, the first three places remained the same, but then came Syd Ring and Alf Taylor, hard chased by Bert Footer. Our Captain must have been running a "snaky" race, as he was about the last out of the field at the start. Congratulations to "Ding-Dong" on finishing the course—and not last, either! Also hearty congratulations to our junior runner, K. N. Wood, on taking the handicap prize; and to Alf Taylor and Syd Ring, who were placed second and third in the sealed handicap. I believe most of the actual times recorded in the Championship were a shade faster than last year. † Dead Heat. Pos. Name Club Act. Time Start H'cap Time Pos. in H'cap 1 A. W. items.s: THE 5 MILES JUNIOR CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the club five miles junior cross-country championship for the "Savage" Shield on December 21st, won by E. Stimpson from D. Martin and G. R. Chantler. On December 21st our "Junior" Championship was held to decide who should become the holder of the "Savage" Shield for the ensuing year; and the paucity of entrants was more than compensated for by the quality of the racing. George Chantler (the holder), Dave Martin, Ed Stimpson and Ken Wood were always close together; but in the closing stages Stimpson found a little extra speed to finish nine seconds ahead of Martin. Chantler followed three seconds later, with Wood another 12 seconds away. Thus the fourth man finished only 24 seconds behind the winner, and shows what a splendid chance we have of retaining the "Southern" Junior title in February. We have, of course, three members of last year's winning team still available, and backed up by Wood, Chamberlain, Quackenbos, Merryman and Pointer, they can scarcely fail to do well. It is a source of great satisfaction to us to know that we have such splendid talent maturing and fitting itself for the senior ranks in due course. m. s. 1 E. Stimpson 30 16 2 D. Martin 30 25 3 G. Bird, 3 miles walk won by L. F. Bailey. Our annual Boxing Day meeting was held at Battersea Park Track, as usual, and the track was very heavy, owing to the continuous rains. The entries for the 120 yards sprint were much better than last year, and when the five heat winners lined up for the final, an expectant crowd awaited the result. T. H. Cannon (11) proved the winner off a mark he will certainly not see again, with F. W. Pritchard (8), second, and K. J. Crawford (10) third. Our young Junior Sprint Champion, B. Saunders, qualified for the final but was unplaced, as was Frank Webb. The 2 Miles Run proved a good race and after George Still had shown the way in the early stages, A. T. A. Jordan (300) took the lead only to lose it in a thrilling struggle down the straight to A. A. Bird (250). J. C. Edwards (350) finished third, with A. H. Beaumont (280) 4th, G. Still (650) 5th. A. R. Shaw ran well off 95 yds. to finish 6th. A. W. Penny, our Empire Games 6 Miles Champion, turned out but was content to finish 12th, his time being 10 mins. 5 secs. The time of the winner was 9 mins. 43 secs., and considering the heavy going this was quite a sound performance. In the 3 Miles Walk we saw a fine performance by Len Fletcher who, off 20 yds., finished second to L. F. Bailey (600). Charlie Speechley (275) gained third place with J. E. e: Surrey County Junior Cross Country Championships
items.s: THE COUNTY CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIPS. Report and results of the 1935-36 county cross-country championships: Belgrave's fourth successive Surrey team win with Arthur Penny individual champion, Cadogan A.C. third in Middlesex with E. S. Stimpson winning the junior race, Pat Parker Sussex champion, and the club third in the Surrey junior championship. The Surrey race, held at Epsom, provided us with our fourth successive win, and once again we supplied the individual champion. We has expected to do both of these things, but Arthur Penny had a gruelling race with S. C. Belton (Surrey A.C.) in order to regain the Surrey title. Belton was a real thorn in Arthur's side, and it was only in the closing stages that our man was able to open up a small gap and hold it to the end. Third came the old warrior, Bert Footer, running one of his "waiting" races, and showing that will be with the leaders when the "Southern" and "National" come along. Our third man was Tom Carter, in 8th position. He ran very creditably in view of his short preparation, following on a minor accident which had put him out of the game for nearly a month. Next for us came Syd Ring, striving to put every second possible between himself and the following men; then Bert Cook, the evergreen; and "Mick" Walker. We thus finished our six in the first 19 scoring positions. Surrey A.C.'s sixth man scored 21, so it will be seen that our win was by no means an easy one. Every man had to do his bit to enable us to score 53 points to the 77 of Surrey A.C. It will be remembered that it was in this race last year that Arthur Penny fractured his meta-tarsial bone, which resulted in him being an onlooker until this season started. It was pleasing to see him re-assume one of his old titles and show that he is as good as ever. In the Middlesex race held from Enfield Lock, our members competing encountered a real cross-country course, with more than its share of hills and mud. In the last two years Cadogan A.C. (whose members are all first-claim Belgrave Harriers) had won the team title; but this time had to strike their flag, not altogether unexpectedly. The team was well-beaten by Southgate H. and Polytechnic H., and next year our lads will be all out to regain their lost title. In the absence of D. and R. Patience abroad on Foreign service we knew things would be more difficult, but with Ginty unable to run owing to ankle trouble, and Saunders arriving late following a motor-cycle breakdown, Cadogan A.C. were certainly up against it! The course was certainly not to Arthur Allum's liking, and Alf Taylor took over Arthur's usual role of leading the team in. In all the circumstances third team placing must be considered creditable, and is sure to spur our men on to something better next year. The Senior race had been preceded by the Junior event over five miles, and in this E. S. Stimpson distinguished himself by showing splendid form throughout, and winning comfortably. He should help our seniors along next year. Our only other runner in this was H. M. Quackenbos, who was placed 16th of the 51 starters—quite a good effort. Pat Parker carried off the Sussex individual title which was competed for at Hassocks ,and Bert Shaw took fourth place in the Kent championship. items.label: February 1936
items.sum: Preview of the club's remaining 1936 winter fixtures: a social run with Herne Hill, the South of Thames championship, Southern and National (English) cross-country championships, the Round Ilford Relay, the club 5 miles road race and the Brighton Relay.
e: South of Thames Cross Country Championship
items.s: WINDING UP THE WINTER SEASON. Preview of the club's remaining 1936 winter fixtures: a social run with Herne Hill, the South of Thames championship, Southern and National (English) cross-country championships, the Round Ilford Relay, the club 5 miles road race and the Brighton Relay. On February 1st we are visiting the Herne Hill Harriers for a social run from the Grandstand, Epsom Downs. The surrounding country will by now be quite familiar to our boys; but it is a fine, healthy spot for running, and I recommend it to any of our members who have as yet not sampled it. On February 8th we have the South of Thames 7 Miles C.C. Championship which will be held at Dartford. The last time this race was held there, Bert Footer won the individual title, while our team was placed second in the team race. We hope to go one better this time by securing first place in the team event, although Reading A.C. appear to have an excellent chance of improving on their second place of last year. Unfortunately, most of our cracks are barred from competing, but we have some most promising talent in our junior ranks and know that our boys will not fail through lack of effort. We have a fixture with St. George's Services A.C. on February 15th. Our Surrey Juniors have already been over the course, which is from the L.C.C. Technical School Playing Fields, Grand Drive, Raynes Park. Our team will be of Junior strength and this should give those who are not concerned with our Senior teams a chance of competition late in the season. February 22nd is Southern Counties Day, and both the Senior and Junior races will be held at Sandown Park. The last time the race was held here was in 1886, when the field numbered 181 competitors. This year the field for the Junior race will exceed that number, while over 300 runners are likely to be seen in the Senior event, a sure proof of the growing popularity of cross-country running as a sport. The surrounding country should make for an interesting race and our lads should not be at a disadvantage over this type of course. It should be a most hectic fight between Surrey A.C., the holders, and the "Bels"; and with memories of our one-point defeat last year, our lads can be relied upon to go all out to avenge that reverse. Our Junior team is if anything stronger than last year, and we should certainly retain our title of Southern Junior Champions. Ted Stimpson is running brilliantly, and with Dave Martin, George Chantler, K. N. Wood and J. W. Chamberlain to give their support, they should improve on last year's score. Travelling arrangements will be published at a later date, and will also be placed on the notice board at the "Rising Sun." Spectators should have a fine view of both races and we hope our followers will make the journey. For the following two weeks we have training runs at Wimbledon, when our team will be having their final preparation for the National race on March 14th. THE ENGLISH C.C. CHAMPIONSHIP, of which we are holders, will be held over a 10 miles course in Alderley Park, Cheshire, on March 14th, at 3-15 p.m. I hope that many of our followers will make the journey. It is surprising how it helps to hear a word of encouragement every now and again, especially in a race over 10 miles. Birchfield Harriers will strain every sinew to regain their lost honours; while Surrey A.C. and Salford Harriers are also sure to be well to the fore. This race was held at Alderley Edge in 1933, and Bert Footer and Arthur Penny came in together in 4th position. If they can repeat that performance (and on present form it looks highly likely) we shall have made a good start for team honours. Jim Ginty has now commenced training, and although we shall miss Dan Patience, who is in Egypt; Tom Carter, Alf Taylor and Harry Shields are showing form that gives every promise of their repeating last year's magnificent performance. It is a pity that Pat Parker will not be eligible for our team, nor of course Les Cohen; but even so I am confident that our lads can show the athletic world that Belgrave are supreme over the country. On March 21st will be held the Round Ilford Relay race, of which we are the holders, and at the time of writing it is uncertain what the composition of our team will be. I am sure our "B" team enjoyed their run last year and it may be decided to let them have a crack at the others on their own. A fortnight later, April 4th, we are holding our usual end-of-the-season 5 Miles Road race at Wimbledon. We have a Sealed Handicap open to all members in conjunction with this race; and it serves for those who have kept in steady training all through the Winter season. The result of the scratch race is also used when selecting our team for the Brighton Relay race, which takes place three weeks later. All those who wish to be considered for this race should make a point of being at Wimbledon on April 4th. On referring to the fixture card you will notice that the date of our Road Race has been altered, but this is owing to the Brighton Relay date being brought forward. APRIL 25th, Brighton Relay Day. I had better not say London to Brighton, as according to what we hear the race is due to start anywhere between Mitcham and Dorking. One thing is certain, and that is that the Commissioner of Police has forbidden it to start from Westminster, as in years past. It seems rather a pity, as it robs the event of the interest taken in the carrying by the runners of a letter from the Lord Mayor of London to his counterpart at Brighton. I expect Joe Binks, with his usual slick publicity methods will soon get another to replace this, but at the time of writing all we know is that the race will be held, but that's about all. Anyway, sailors don't care, so why should we? One thing we do know, that this race provides a good day's outing for both young and old; and I am sure all our lads look forward to it as one of the season's most sporting events. Incidentally, if our boys can win again this year they will put up a record by winning the event three years in succession. Birchfield have twice had successive wins but so far no club has done the treble, so up the "Bels," and do your stuff! Entries and enquiries should be sent to— E. A. DUFFETT, Asst. Hon. Sec., 10, Barrow Road, Waddon, Surrey. items.label: February 1936
items.sum: Humorous account by A. S. Lindsey of the club's third Social of the season on December 14th, with the burlesque show "Belgrave Nights" or "East of Wapping" starring A. A. Harley as Sheik El Red.
items.s: "BELGRAVIAN NIGHTS." Humorous account by A. S. Lindsey of the club's third Social of the season on December 14th, with the burlesque show "Belgrave Nights" or "East of Wapping" starring A. A. Harley as Sheik El Red. The third Social of the season was held on December 14th. A fair number stayed to tea and were supplemented later by others eager to dance, and to see the show which we were promised. Unfortunately, the band engaged was late, and things had to be got going; and this is where our Hon. Secretary, Wally, stepped up. He did some good work on the ivories, assisted with great gusto by the company present. Eventually the band materialised, and after a short period of dancing we came to the attraction of the evening—"Belgrave Nights" or "East of Wapping." The curtain rose (if one may use the term) depicting the splendour of the East, with Sheik El Red (A. A. Harley) reclining on a divan, looking a veritable Bluebeard all gone bloodshot. (Note: in our last presentation, "Love in Bloom," it will be remembered that our esteemed Hon. Editor was then only a back-row girl. Well done, Red!). At the Sheik's side towered his Nubian (bleached) slave, Ali Ben Mai, a colossal heap of flesh, but none the less an honest fellow, who calls a blade a blade. At the Master's bidding, Ali ushered in the Court musicians (Jack and Charlie) who gave a good account of themselves on the accordions, and were awarded long and uproarious applause. Next came a slave girl (Percy Wright), a beautiful maiden from the East (End!), but with Ali it was a case of see blondes and bust! Sallying forth, he literally proceeded to knock the stuffing out of the maiden. After this bout (which Ali won by three throws to nil), the slave girl entertained us with a snake dance; a string of best beef sausages taking the place of the snake. To keep the Royal pot a-boiling, Ali, with a few passes of his (t)rusty blade, persuaded the Court singer (T. Cotton) to entertain. Of course, Tom always goes down well. Unfortunately, you can't keep a good man down for long! After this, the Court musicians got busy again, and to the strains of Eastern music, the Neverwere Dancers entered, presenting a very native dance dedicated to their patron, St. Vitus. This part of the show was under the personal supervision of Miss J. Parsons, whom we all thank for her patience and interest. An easier task would be training elephants to walk the tight-rope, and the chances of success would be greater! Alf. Taylor and A. A. Bird should go far; I am on safe ground in saying the like has never been seen before! "Mick" Walker and "Snaky" Webb, whose dancing reputations are far-flung, should play opposite one another, more often if possible. Ring, the Ruthless, gave a great exhibition of Eastern passion in contrast to his partner, Cecil Penny, who danced with utter abandon. La Josephine, and our friend Ali, put in some fine work, although I am inclined to think the scales were faked when they weighed in! The performance was seasonably concluded by El Red distributing presents on behalf of generous-hearted Belgravians to their fellow-members and friends—the sweetest thoughts. Some of the gifts touched us deeply, but owing to the number of presents, and the limited space allowed me, I must leave it to the Hon. Editor's discretion as to which presents call for special mention! The Hon. Editor regrets . . . . . A. S. Lindsey A. S. LINDSEY "Our Dramatic Critic" A. S. LINDSEY A. A. Harley A. A. items.label: May 1936
items.sum: Obituary of W. A. (Bill) Rice, Track Captain and Social Hon. Secretary, who died on 25 April 1936 aged 31.
items.s: Obituary of W. A. (Bill) Rice, Track Captain and Social Hon. Secretary, who died on 25 April 1936 aged 31. It is with the utmost regret, and with a profound sense of our great loss, that we announce the death of our Track Captain, and Social Hon. Secretary, W. A. Rice. Bill had endeared himself to everyone within the Club. For twelve years his influence had been a very real thing to us, and as runner, Committee-man, painstaking Social Hon. Secretary, and diligent Track Captain, he contributed much towards the progress the Club has made during the last decade. Athletics is not merely a matter of championships and performances. It is the means of introducing one to some splendid sportsmen of sterling character, and there are many of us, sorrowful though we may be at the moment, who were glad to have had the privilege of Bill's friendship. His personal qualities meant much to us and the Club he loved, and his memory will be cherished by all who knew him. Bill's thoughts were constantly with the Club throughout his long illness, and his interest was as alive as when he was out and about with us. Even as life ebbed, in his delirious thoughts he lived again his races on the Club's behalf; and, on April 25th, as the Brighton Relay (in which he had captained previous victorious teams) drew to a close, so did our beloved friend's life, at the early age of 31 years. The Club was represented by a dozen or more friends at the funeral, anxious to pay last respects to one who meant so much to all of us. Death has robbed us; but we cannot be robbed of pleasurable memories of a splendid friend, a genial personality, and a hard worker in every phase of the Club's activities. We extend our deepest sympathy to Mrs. Rice, and to the relatives and friends, upon their very great loss. W. A. Rice W. A. Rice Track Captain and Social Hon. Secretary; died 25 April 1936 aged 31; had captained victorious Brighton Relay teams Mrs. Rice Mrs. Rice family of W. A. Rice London to Brighton Relay

items.s: Obituary of young member E. H. M. Williams, a schoolmaster and South of Thames Junior cross-country champion, who died on 25 April 1936 aged 24, with thanks for messages of sympathy. On April 25th also, another young friend, E. H. M. Williams, passed away. His death at the age of 24 years is little short of a tragedy. In his two years of membership, he had established himself as a great favourite with us, and we were all delighted last November when our young schoolmaster friend won the South of Thames C.C. Association's Junior Championship. His running career had seemed full of promise, and his participation in the Club's strolling, social, as well as racing activities, had gained him many friends. We had expected these friendships to last for many years, and the tragic termination of Marshall's life fills us all with very deep regret. It was not possible for the Club to be represented at the funeral, which took place in North Wales; but a floral tribute was sent from the Club. Our profound sympathy goes out to our friend's parents and relatives in their time of sorrow. In his two years with us he had enhanced the Club name, and we have lost another fine personality and splendid clubman. * * * * * We have received several expressions of sympathy from Associations and Clubs, for which we extend our sincere thanks. items.s: THIS AND THAT. Club notes: third successive Brighton Relay win, fifth R.W.A. Junior 10 miles walk team win, Honours Badges for Carter, Churcher and Fletcher, new club ties and track vests, welcoming new members, and a call for field-event athletes. Heartiest congratulations to those responsible for gaining the Club's third successive win in the Brighton Relay—a feat never recorded by any other club. Well done! * * * * * And, well-walked! and more hearty congratulations to the team that won the R.W.A. Junior 10 miles Championship. This is our fifth win—and this again is a feat not yet accomplished by any other club. * * * * * We congratulate C. T. Carter, C. E. Churcher and A. L. Fletcher upon gaining their Club Honours Badges. Carter qualified in the "Southern," Churcher in the "Junior" Walk, and Len Fletcher by gaining first-class standard in the recent A.A.A. 7 miles Championship. His actual position was fourth, and at this meeting Tom Carter ran one of his best races yet in finishing third in the 10 miles Run Championship in very fast time. * * * * * One of the new Club ties at 3/- is just the thing to complete your Summer ensemble, and they may be obtained from the Hon. Treasurer (address on page 1). He will also be glad to receive outstanding subscriptions. * * * * * Within a short time a new sleeveless light-weight vest will be available for track use, and this also may be had from our Hon. Treasurer. * * * * * At this time of the year we are happy to welcome many new members, and they are asked to get in touch with the Club officials as quickly as possible, and make themselves known. Old members, for their part, are asked to do all in their power to advise and help the newcomer. A friendly word and a little practical help are greatly appreciated when one is a newcomer to a sport ; and it is hoped that all members of some years' standing will keep their eyes open for new talent, and assist wherever possible. * * * * * Our Field Events Captain, W. Sutton, would be glad to welcome any athlete interested in Field Events. This section has already made a fine start in the S.A.A.L, competition, which, of course, we won last year. C. T. Carter C. T. e: Belgrave Harriers 10 miles Walk Championship (Murphy Shield)
items.s: THE TEN MILES WALK CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the club's ten miles walk championship for the Murphy Shield, won by Len Fletcher from Harry Churcher, with Bill Snell and W. Urry taking the handicap awards. The annual contest for the right to hold the "Murphy" Shield for the ensuing year attracted a fair field, including a past holder in Len Fletcher, and the holder, Don Brown. It was soon apparent that Fletcher and Harry Churcher had designs upon the championship, and their rivalry carried them away from the rest of the field; Len winning by a few yards, with the holder filling third position. Bill Snell, who has showed much improved form this year, took the sealed handicap award; and it was pleasing to see a comparative newcomer in W. Urry qualify for the second award. He continues to improve and should help our teams in due course. Several prominent Club men were prevented from turning out in this event, owing to colds, etc., which always seem so prevalent in January, and so robbed the race of some of its interest, although the race between the first two men could not have been improved upon, whatever the entry. items.s: THE LONDON TRANSPORT OPEN WALK. Report and results of the London Transport Open Walk at Bellingham, where Belgrave won the scratch team race over Surrey Walking Club and the handicap team award. As usual, our walkers supported the Bellingham Walk in good numbers, and tackled the two-and-a-half laps of hills, gasworks, and housing estate with optimism. Our men were soon prominent, and eventually we had two in the first three places, and our first-choice team scored an easy win over Surrey Walking Club. Three members of the winning scratch team, plus Bill Snell, who took second prize in the handicap, formed the winning handicap team, and altogether we made a most successful visit to Bellingham. items.s: THE ASHCOMBE A.C. OPEN WALK. Report and results of the Ashcombe A.C. Open Walk in Richmond Park, postponed by fog from 15 February to 14 March, where Belgrave's A and B teams took second and third handicap team prizes. This event, fixed for February 15th, had to be postponed owing to dense fog which enveloped the roads in Richmond Park and rendered racing dangerous. Our Ashcombe friends decided to make a second attempt on March 14th, and entries were re-opened. As usual, we had a good muster, and again we supplied two of the first three placed men. There is no scratch team race included in this event (only a set of prizes for the fastest unplaced team in the handicap), and in the handicap team event our Surrey W.C. friends were successful. Our efforts to scheme two teams into placings were successful, the A's taking second place and the B's third prizes. In addition, Bob Readman took third prize in the individual handicap and so brought his tally of awards up to five in four open races. We are expecting big things of him at 10 and 20 miles next season. Pos. Act. Time Allce. H'cap Time 1. G. T. Galloway (S.W.C.) 76 36 1 10 75 26 2. A. L. Fletcher (Bel. A.) 77 9 1 10 75 29 3. D. E. items.label: May 1936
items.sum: T. C. Jones's report and results of the R.W.A. Junior 10 miles walking championship at Colindale on 7 March 1936, in which Belgrave's A team beat Leicester W.C. by 5 points for the club's fifth win in the race, with C. E. Churcher second.
items.s: R.W.A. "JUNIOR" 10 MILES WALKING CHAMPIONSHIP. T. C. Jones's report and results of the R.W.A. Junior 10 miles walking championship at Colindale on 7 March 1936, in which Belgrave's A team beat Leicester W.C. by 5 points for the club's fifth win in the race, with C. E. Churcher second. The "Junior," held on the 7th March from headquarters of the Metropolitan Police A.A. at Colindale, once again saw us win this race, but only after an exciting struggle with Leicester W.C. At about 6½ miles (which was the first time I had been able to see the competitors since the start, and then only after taking a bus ride) Leicester were leading us by 18 points. Staines (Leicester) was leading the field, Charlie Churcher being our first man in 6th position, Percy Wright and Jack Rutland together 10th and 11th, and Charlie Redgrave 26th. Len Storey was leading the "B" team in 27th position, Charlie Speechley 29th (he was "gonged" a little while after this) and C. F. D. Sutton ("B") 33rd. Dunlop W.C. were third with 61 points only 8 points—behind us. Our boys during the next 3 miles put in some fine walking, and when I next checked the scores with about half-a-mile to go, Charlie Churcher had moved up to 2nd place, about 150 yards behind Staines; Percy Wright, 4th; Jack Rutland, 8th; and Charlie Redgrave, 18th. We were only 1 point behind Leicester, with Surrey W.C. now in 3rd place. C. F. D. Sutton was now 26th, leading the "B" team. How well our boys walked in the last half-mile can be gauged from the fact that six points were gained. Charlie Churcher was beaten by only 8 seconds; Percy Wright, 4th; Jack Rutland, 7th; and Charlie Redgrave, 16th; making us winners from Leicester by 5 points. Very appropriate that we should win again in the year of office of Mr. F. G. Thomson as President of the R.W.A.! Our boys were particularly pleased with their win over the most difficult course, for it brought the Club's total of wins in this race to five—a record superior to that of any other club in the country. The hilly nature of the course gave rise to many disqualifications and we suffered in common with other clubs. There is little doubt, however, that we have in our reserve strength a team that will go very near winning again next year. Our "B" team did well to fill 11th position. As a last word, let us pay tribute to gallant losers—Leicester W.C. Nine times out of ten their score is a winning one. This year, second place was their lot. m. s. 1. A. items.s: THE 20 MILES' WALK CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and results of the club 20 miles walk championship, run as a match against a Metropolitan Police W.C. team made up mostly of Belgrave members, won by T. W. Green with Belgrave winning the match 38 points to 40 (the printed handicap positions give 11 to both R. Martin and L. R. Spooner). A match v. Metropolitan Police W.C. was arranged in connection with our Club Championship, their team for this purpose consisting, with one exception, of our own Club members, also in quest of Club honours. All of which sounds rather involved, but actually is very simple, as a glance at the result will show. Our course, which returns almost to the starting point at 8, 11 and 17 miles, once again provided several walkers with an opportunity to "cut it short"—which they accepted. Others kept on...... on...... on...... Tommy Green was the first to reach the finishing post, closely followed by Fred Rickards. Fred, who was winning this race years ago, seems fitter than ever, and we may confidently expect him to demand the attention of the selectors when our Olympic athletes are chosen. It would be a great compliment to our Club and to Police walking if Rickards was chosen, and we know he has the ability and temperament necessary. Third man was Charlie Churcher, a welcome surprise. His first attempt at the distance is full of promise, and he definitely strengthens our team. The next two, Bentley and Bidgood, seemed a little lazy, which means they are saving themselves for future events; and sixth came Bob Readman, who continues to improve and promises to do well. Urry also did well at his first attempt; and in Reeve we have another member who should show up well next season. Churcher's brilliant form earned him first prize in the sealed handicap, with Readman second, and a well-deserving case third. The match v. Police, scoring six aside, gave us a two points win, as the appended result shows. Also started : A. L. Fletcher, W. A. Treacher, R. G. Hillier, B. H. Clark, C. G. Pattenden, G. H. Boddington, F. W. items.s: THE 10 MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and results of the club 10 miles cross-country championship, won from the start by Arthur Penny from the holder H. E. Footer, with C. T. Carter first on handicap; 27 finished. A field of 30 faced the starter, Mr. A. E. Macher (Junr.), who paid us one of his infrequent visits to start the race for the Championship for which his father donated the Shield. This was, perhaps, the foundation stone to the present high standard to which our runners have now attained over 10 miles. Previous to the institution of this race, it was very difficult to get the team to train over ten miles, so that when the "Southern" came along our men were always outclassed. The result of the race was never in doubt, barring accidents, as Arthur Penny took the lead from the start, and gradually drew away from the field, eventually winning as he pleased. At the half-distance he was 55 secs. in front of Carter, with Parker next, having a very bad time, and hereabouts he retired. Bert Footer came next. Soon after this, Bert forged ahead to pass Carter, Flower came up from 10th position to 7th to displace Allum, and Shields dropped back a couple of places. These positions were maintained to the finish. 27 finished, which is perhaps the biggest field for a number of years. Although the weather was better than that of last year, there was a slight drizzle of rain and the course was on the heavy side; but this should not have accounted for the race being won in one minute slower time than that of Footer last year. items.label: May 1936
items.sum: G. Doubleday's report and results of the South of the Thames senior cross-country championship at Littlebrook Farm, Dartford, won by F. Close (Reading A.C.), with Belgrave winning the Dewar Shield on 117 points and regaining the Sir J. Colman Cup.
e: South of the Thames Cross Country Championships
items.s: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES "SENIOR." G. Doubleday's report and results of the South of the Thames senior cross-country championship at Littlebrook Farm, Dartford, won by F. Close (Reading A.C.), with Belgrave winning the Dewar Shield on 117 points and regaining the Sir J. Colman Cup. This race was held from Littlebrook Farm, Dartford, and on the last occasion it was held there Bert Footer was first home. Although most of our "cracks" were barred from this race, we fielded a useful team, our chief rivals being Reading A.C., who included in their team F. Close, the then-reigning National Champion. The sun had thawed the surface of the frost-bound ground, to render it very fast in places. It was a sunny day, although there was a nasty wind blowing. After two laps of the starting field, the runners had strung out. Our Junior Champion, Ted Stimpson, was in the first 10; Alec Patience and Syd Ring were lying handy in the early twenties, with the rest of ours strung out to about the eighties. Two of our men were already in trouble. Marshall Williams found an injured foot a handicap, and Cecil Penny, just after the start, injured one of his legs and seemed to be running with difficulty. After one large lap, our men seemed to be settling down, and after the second, we seemed sure of a place. Stimpson was now 8th, running confidently with speed and style. Micky Walker had come up from the fifties and, running powerfully, overhauled Ring who, handicapped by his light build, experienced difficulties with the wind, and appeared to be losing ground. The last lap began to find some of the competitors out, for the course seemed well over seven miles. F. Close was first home, followed by A. C. Stansbury (Ranelagh). Stimpson sprinted up from 7th to 6th place—a magnificent performance. Patience found his form and improved eleven places on last year's performance, to finish 10th. Walker ran powerfully to be 19th, and Ring split the 3rd and 4th Reading men, to finish 22nd. The position of the teams seemed slightly in favour of Reading, although we both had four men home. But two runners in Claret and Gold appeared in the next group and sprinted round the last bend into the funnel—E. G. Saunders and Frank Webb finished 28th and 32nd, to complete our six. So we won the Championship, scoring 117 pts. to Reading's 153 pts., having picked up 50 places on the last lap. Our next four men—George Chantler, Bert Mitchell, Dave Martin and Bert Jordan—soon closed in. Williams and Penny, who normally would have been battling up the front for a place in the scoring six, ran on pluckily, intent upon finishing, to help the Club to score a double victory by winning the Cup for the lowest score of the complete team of twelve. Both deserved our warm applause for finishing and enabling the Club to regain the "Sir J. Colman" Cup. The "Dewar" Shield for the team championship has only been in our hands once before (1929); but it must be remembered that our Southern and English Championship placings in recent years have barred many of our best runners from participating in this race. Two or three men each year have placed themselves outside the clauses of eligibility laid down in the rules; and made our task of building a winning team in this race more and more difficult. Heartiest congratulations to our winning team of this year for surmounting these difficulties and providing our team selectors with a further set for Season 1936—1937! 1. F.
