items.label: February 1937
items.sum: Account, by the Hon. Editor with parts by Charlie Jones and Doubleday, of Belgrave's first team trip abroad, to the U.S.M.'s international cross-country race near Paris on 19 January 1937 (as printed), which Belgrave won with 51 points, Parker 3rd and Penny 4th.
items.s: AU CROSS DU METRO. Account, by the Hon. Editor with parts by Charlie Jones and Doubleday, of Belgrave's first team trip abroad, to the U.S.M.'s international cross-country race near Paris on 19 January 1937 (as printed), which Belgrave won with 51 points, Parker 3rd and Penny 4th. The Hon. Editor begins. Les Belgrave Harriers gagnent très facilement le challenge par équipes en classant leurs six coureurs dans les seize premiers . . . . but enough of that! Let's start at the beginning. Two months ago we were honoured by an invitation to compete in an international cross-country race to be held near Paris on Sunday, January 19th. The invitation was, of course, forwarded to us through the International Board of the A.A.A. and in consultation with the English Cross-country Union; and our Committee, recognising the implied compliment, decided to accept our first invitation to compete as a team abroad. Accordingly ten runners (H. E. Footer, J. Parker, L. J. Cohen, J. W. Kemp, H. W. Shields, A. W. Penny, C. T. Carter, E. S. Stimpson, A. E. Taylor, A. R. Shaw), three officials (W. L. Bayliss, H. Parker, A. A. Harley), and six supporters (T. C. Jones, W. Sutton, J. Chamberlain, G. S. Doubleday, N. Isaacs, J. St. Leger) made the crossing via Newhaven—Dieppe and duly arrived at Paris, where they were met by M. Chauvet, President of the Athletic Section of the U.S.M., the promoting club, and M. Girard, whose kind assistance as interpreter and guide throughout our visit were greatly appreciated. And here let me explain that U.S.M. is an abbreviated form of Union Sportive Metropolitain, our hosts and the promoters of the events. This club is the sports organisation of the "Underground" railways of Paris, and, since its formation in 1928, has performed creditably in many branches of sport. In addition to catering for the male and female employees, special arrangements are made for the younger element to enjoy physical culture and games. The U.S.M. regularly fields 12 football teams, four rugby teams, eight basket ball teams (three of which are for women), and also practices athletics and cross-country running, walking, rowing, swimming, cycling, tennis, boxing, gymnastics and other sports and games. Truly a very comprehensive range of activities. To resume, after disgressing somewhat: our party was conducted to the hotel, and after a wash and dinner, sallied forth to see something of Paris, the team being under orders to return early and retire! Next morning, our President and myself were awakened by a ringing telephone, and M. Vrolix, President of the U.S.M., bade us "Welcome" and arranged to be at our hotel a little later. Breakfast over, a representative of the Ministry of Sport waited on us, and on the arrival of M. Vrolix, a coach was ordered by telephone and we were shown the main points of interest in Paris, and then proceeded to the magnificent quarters of L'Union Sportive Metropolitain at Le Croix de Berny, about twelve miles outside Paris itself. While the team had a look at the course, the Club officials and supporters lunched in the pavilion in distinguished company, which included the Minister of Education and his wife, the Minister of Sport and several other distinguished Frenchmen. Our President sat cheek-by-jowl with the notabilities and conducted himself with dignity—but seemed a little off his food! Maybe his thoughts were twenty-four hours in retrospect! The U.S.M. Sports Ground is splendidly appointed, with fine dressing rooms, a large gymnasium, many football, rugby and basket-ball pitches, and a running track. It was on the track that racing started and finished. A junior race preceded the main event, but we were not represented in this. It had been expected that Ted Stimpson would carry our colours in this event; but it was discovered that the French definition of a junior and ours were not in accord, and so it was arranged that he should run in the senior event. At the close of the junior race, the seniors were assembled and each team trotted round the track and were presented by loudspeaker to the crowd. Then the line-up and start. The course consisted of four laps of very sticky grassland, returning to the track for the beginning of each lap; the runners being in view practically the whole time. Twenty-four teams were entered, and there was a good complement of runners. The start was a very, very fast one. At the half-mile it is doubtful if we had a man inside the first fifty positions. Then Pat Parker decided that it was time the Belgrave colours were taken further forward, and he gained dozens of places, closely followed by Tom Carter. At the end of the first lap they occupied sixth and seventh places. A few positions later came Les Cohen, with Bert Footer and Arthur Penny together in the early twenties, and our others not far behind. Charlie Jones carries on. On the second lap Parker moved up to fifth behind Guiomar, Bernard (Metro), and two Moroccan Soldiers of S.A. Verdun. Carter was 6th, followed by Penny 12th, Footer 14th, Cohen 15th, Taylor 17th, Shaw 21st, Kemp 24th, Stimpson 32nd and Harry Shields 33rd. The next lap showed a great improvement in our placings and we appeared to have a great chance of winning easily, for Parker was now third only about sixty yards behind the leaders. Penny and Footer had moved up to 5th and 6th respectively, closely followed by Carter 8th, Cohen 14th, Taylor 15th, Shaw 16th. On the last lap the positions were maintained and Parker eventually finished 3rd a short way behind the two Frenchmen, Penny 4th (having passed a man down the straight), Footer 6th, Carter 7th, Cohen 15th, Taylor 16th (giving us a score of 51 points, Shaw 17th, Stimpson 21st, Kemp, 29th and Shields 44th completing our team. The second team were the Moroccans (with a score of 130 points), third the Brussells team (who won the race last year) with 156 points, and fourth our hosts, Metro, with 157 points. Our team must be congratulated on the fine performance in this race, having worthily upheld the traditions of English cross-country running, and also brought the name of the Club into the limelight on the Continent. We received a fine trophy in the form of an athlete in bronze, and our first seven received prizes for their efforts. Doubleday, in at the finish. So, as you all know, Belgrave won their first Continental cross-country race. Although, so we understand, some of the leading Paris runners and clubs were absent (we would have liked to have seen them there) we can have nothing but praise and admiration for our team packing, and the support of our non-scoring men. One point of interest which arises is the fact that although our men are training for 10 miles they can still compete with the best at six miles. After the presentation of the prizes, we all crowded into a "tram" to take us to the "Metro," whence back to the hotel, to place the trophy in a place of honour, and to have dinner. During dinner, M. Vrolix called to say "Au revoir," and we were glad to have the opportunity of saying "Thank you!" to him and his organisation for the splendid time we had enjoyed. Most of us came back on Sunday night, having a very turbulent crossing. Those who stayed in Paris another night had an even worse crossing—so they say,—but "Curtain please!" But before it falls, on behalf of the Club, our sincere thanks to the U.S.M. and its officials. Also to those who served our Club so well as runners, officials and supporters on our first athletic trip abroad. May we end with one French word? Encore! H. E. Footer H. E. items.s: ASHCOMBE A.C. and T.V.H. at WIMBLEDON. C. T. Cohen first, plus the full result and sealed handicap won by R. J. Powell. By C. T. CARTER. Yo! heave ho! me hearties! or words to that effect. No, I'm not writing of the Bay of Biscay, but of Wimbledon when there is water about. After a fairly fast start, Les Cohen was in the lead at the Brook, but Art Penny was closing on him, and a Thames Valley man was in third position. At the Windmill, Cohen still led with a six seconds margin over Penny and, with our other men following one another in quick succession, ensured us of an easy team win. Our congratulations go to R. J. Powell, a young member of great promise, who won the sealed handicap. Another junior member, Merryman, was second, and J. H. Chantler took third place. items.label: February 1937
items.sum: H. W. Shields's report of the South of the Thames junior cross-country race on Epsom Downs, where Belgrave were second team behind the Royal Navy and Marines and K. N. Wood was third, with the result and team scores.
e: South of the Thames Junior Cross Country
items.s: "SOUTH OF THE THAMES" JUNIOR RACE. H. W. Shields's report of the South of the Thames junior cross-country race on Epsom Downs, where Belgrave were second team behind the Royal Navy and Marines and K. N. Wood was third, with the result and team scores. By H. W. SHIELDS. The thing which always most impresses me about this race is the wonderfully keen support given by members, who seem to turn up in their dozens and make the Downs echo with the cry of "Up the Bels."; so that supporters' shouts from other clubs seem in comparison to be like murmurs. This, I am sure, has had much to do with our truly remarkable performances in this event. We have been placed since 1932, and the previous years show an equally fine record, in spite of the fact that numerous men are "barred" each year. Anyhow, to get on with the race. After a very good start the runners struck out for that very hilly piece of Epsom Downs by the cottages, where we were able to take stock of our chances. At this point we had Murdoch in the first half-dozen, with Clements, Beaumont and Wood in the early twenties. From here it was obvious we should be placed. On the second lap round, Wood was moving up amazingly. Clements was also passing men rapidly. Beaumont was still running strongly, occupying about the same position as before, with Murdoch, although dropping slightly, running very well as our fourth man. From the appended result it will be seen that our men put up a very good show, especially when it is remembered that many were competing in their first race of any importance. Wood merits our hearty congratulations upon his placing in this event. We trust that in due course he will run similarly in senior events. RESULT. TEAM SCORES. Pos. Name m. s. 3 K. N. items.s: NOVEMBER 21st. Short report of a cross-country fixture at Wimbledon on 21 November against Aylesford Paper Mills S.C., the South Staffs. Regt. and the Guards Depot, won easily by Belgrave. On this day we entertained Aylesford Paper Mills S.C.; South Staffs. Regt. and the Guards Depot (Caterham) at Wimbledon. We ran out easy winners of the team event, placing 13 men (headed by L. Cohen) in the first 15 places, the other two being from the Paper Mills. The soldiers turned out in very good numbers and our Hall was well and truly packed. Everyone seemed to enjoy the run, and the tea we provided for the visitors disappeared with wonderful rapidity! May we suggest that cream buns for tea would ease the recruiting problem? L. Cohen L. Ring's report of 13 Belgrave Harriers' visit to Ealing on 28 November, won by Belgrave, with the result; the text gives Belgrave's score as 86 pts. but the team scores give 88 pts. (both as printed). By S. T. RING. On November 28th, 13 Belgrave Harriers visited Ealing, some of the absentees being with Mr. E. J. Holt's team at Cambridge. The Bels started splendidly and for half-a-mile the home runners were well to the front. Bain set a corking pace and opened quite a gap, but over the fields our men gradually picked up. Allum assumed second place, followed by Stimpson, but they were too far behind to make any impression on Bain. Stimpson eventually took second place, and Footer, running through the field, came into fourth place. Final scores were: Belgrave 86 pts., Ealing 126 pts. I noticed, amongst other things, "Sparrow," belying his name, hung up feet first on a stile, and our Social Hon. Secretary and one other "snaking" off to change near a fire. RESULT. e: Belgrave Harriers Seven Miles Cross Country Championship
items.s: THE SEVEN MILES CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Cecil Penny's report of the club Seven Miles cross-country championship, a trial for the Paris team, with comments on the also-rans and the full result with handicap times (as printed, J. C. Edwards's and G. Still's handicap times do not equal actual time minus start). By CECIL PENNY. Two things occurred to me at the start of this race. Firstly, why is it we usually start so late that the majority of the runners complete the course in darkness? Secondly, it's about time a definite starting point was decided on, as this latter differs from year to year. Of what use are times if this is so? The race itself had added interest this year as the boys knew a good showing would enhance their claims for a place in the team to visit Paris. As is usual the cracks set the pace, Penny, Cohen (who is showing improved form this year) leading, Ring, Taylor, Stimpson and Parker being bunched just behind. It's the others I want to mention this time, however—those runners who enter our Championships year after year, their only reward a hard "bashing." "Champion" Smith seemed to enjoy his tussle with our old friend "Doub." Edwards, White, Tommy Morrell (making a come-back) and a not very well-known Bel, Herbert, had a rare battle all the way. Our one and only George Still finished fresher than most of those in front—probably due to Ben carrying him part of the way. They certainly seemed loath to part company. Tobin ran well, and with a year or so of experience behind him, may surprise us. The Patience brothers hardly justified their reputation, due, no doubt, to the fact they had arrived home only a week or so earlier from abroad. Our two most prominent juniors, Stimpson and Wood, ran magnificently in such company. In conclusion, I must express the thoughts of all: how we missed that diminutive figure, red of face, black of hair, running this year! RESULT. items.s: BELGRAVE H. v. EALING H. A. S. Lindsey's report of the cross-country match against Ealing Harriers on December 18th, which Belgrave won easily as a team (72 pts. to 138), with the result. By A. S. LINDSEY. This fixture took place on December 18th, and we had expected a Metropolitan Police team to participate. However, the Proclamation ceremonies demanded the services of many of our old rivals from Imber Court, and they were unable to field a team. Over the first mile the field of thirty runners kept well together, but on coming to the horse-ride, some began to find their feet (others found them also, but with more difficulty !). Despite the burst of Spring-like sunshine, the Clerk of the Weather had put one over us, for in parts the course was like a quagmire. Bain, of Ealing, eventually ran out winner, beating George Chantler by 200 yards or so. Although we did not have our strongest team out, our runners put in some good work in the last mile, and our tenth man finished in 13th position, giving us a very easy team win. The course was somewhat shorter than usual, as the runners went straight out from the start, and omitted the Brook crossing. RESULT. (27 finished). TEAM SCORES. 1 J. Bain E.H. 2 G. Chantler B.H. 3 G. items.s: THE BOXING DAY HANDICAPS. G. Doubleday's report of the club's Boxing Day track handicaps: 120 yards, 2 miles and 3 miles walk. By G. DOUBLEDAY. For those sprinters who keep fit during the winter (and others !) there were four heats in the 120 yards race, the winners proceeding to the final. The starter got them all away first time in the final and Skelley (off 8) broke the worsted, with K. Crawford (8) and A. Mewes (8½) being 2nd and 3rd. F. Simmons was the unlucky fourth. Then came the 2 miles run. This was won by one of our promising juniors, W. Selby, who, making his first track appearance, made good use of his 420 yards start, to win in 9 mins. 19 secs., about 20 yards in front of N. Isaacs (480). L. Herbert showed his versatility by running up from 190 yards to fill third place. In the 3 Miles Walk L. J. Coleman maintained the improvement he seems to show every time out and won easily. He seems destined to become a Club champion in the course of a few years. J. G. Coleman and J. Rutland filled the minor placings. So ended our annual Christmastide track meeting, which goes back to the Club's beginning; although in those days the Embankment had to serve for a track! G. Doubleday G. DOUBLEDAY G. items.s: SURREY COUNTY CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. T. C. Jones's report of the Surrey County cross-country championship at Epsom Downs on 2nd January, won by Belgrave from Surrey A.C. for their tenth win in twelve years, with Belgrave results and team scores (the text has Cohen seventh, the result 8th). By T. C. JONES. The Surrey County Championship was held at Epsom Downs again this year, on the 2nd January. We had a good team entered and had hopes of repeating our win of last year. We were well placed at the start, and after about a mile and a half Hines, of Surrey, was leading, followed by Belton (Surrey), Thorogood (Mitcham), with about nine of ours in the first thirty. At three miles Bert Footer was on Hines' shoulder, having apparently done a bit of "snaky" running when out of sight of the spectators. Penny was next, followed by Carter, Cohen, Ring, and Wood (who won the Surrey Junior Race the week after) in the first twenty places. Our hopes of repeating our win of last year were now very bright; and we next saw the field coming round Tattenham Corner led by Bert Footer, followed by Belton. Then came Hines, Weatherill, Penny fifth, Carter sixth, Cohen seventh, Ring thirteenth, and Wood seventeenth. This scoring enabled us to win comfortably from Surrey A.C., thus making our tenth win in the last twelve years. RESULT. TEAM SCORES. m. s. m. s. 1 H. E. Footer 41 43 19 G. Chantler 44 42 5 A. e: Belgrave Harriers Five Miles Junior Cross Country Championship
items.s: FIVE MILES JUNIOR CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. H. M. Quackenbos's report of the club Five Miles Junior cross-country championship for the "Savage" Shield on December 19th, won by A. F. Clements, with the result (as printed, 6th-placed Powell's time is slower than 7th-placed Field's). By H. M. QUACKENBOS. The "Junior" Championship for the "Savage" Shield, held on December 19th, attracted a larger field than usual; but we were sorry to miss E. S. Stimpson, who was prevented from turning out by business calls. The runners were away in a pack to a slow start and kept well together until they were out of sight. About half-way, Clements managed to open up a gap from Wood and a mile from home had established a lead of two hundred yards, which was never reduced. The leaders were running strongly at this point but positions remained unchanged over the last mile. Clements is improving steadily this season and excelled himself to win in a time which is 16 seconds faster than that of Stimpson last year. Wood was below the brilliant form he has displayed earlier in the season; and Martin, too, was unlucky in having an off-day and failing to improve on his two second places in this race in last years. Herbert agreeably surprised us with his running and will be a valuable addition to our "Southern Junior" team. The above and Lucas will form the nucleus of our team, and backed up by such keen and capable performers as Merryman, Powell; Field, Deadman and Selby, they should regain the "Southern Junior" title. items.sum: H. W. Shields urges new and less able members to attend the club's away cross-country fixtures.
items.s: AWAY FIXTURES. H. W. Shields urges new and less able members to attend the club's away cross-country fixtures. By H. W. SHIELDS. It is with much regret that I have noticed the serious falling-off of members at away fixtures. This falling-off is almost entirely due to members who have recently joined the club, and members who do not consider they have any chance of getting into teams. It is to these members that I wish to address this note. To new members I say, most earnestly, make a habit of attending all away runs. You will soon find how enjoyable it is to know other clubs, members and courses. Don't be afraid you will be too slow. These clubs go to great pains in order to suit you. Remember, races are not all run at Wimbledon and if you are anxious to do well you must get used to as great a variety of courses as possible. Lastly (but not least) you will find there is no better way of getting to know your fellow club-members. To the other type of member I have mentioned, I can assure them that all fixtures are given the most careful attention by the Committee, and great trouble is taken to get fixtures of the right sort. Even if they do not get into teams they can be assured of getting the best out of athletics, both socially and competitively, in this way,—and this is, of course, the happy state of affairs we all desire. H. W. Shields H. W. SHIELDS H. W. SHIELDS Wimbledon

items.label: February 1937
items.sum: Preview of the coming season: cross-country fixtures (South of Thames, Southern Counties, R.W.A. Junior walk, National, club 5 Miles Road race, Brighton Relay), the summer track programme, a possible Club Coach and a welcome to new members, with entries to the Asst. Hon. Sec.
e: South of Thames Cross Country Championship
items.s: LOOKING TO THE FUTURE ! Preview of the coming season: cross-country fixtures (South of Thames, Southern Counties, R.W.A. Junior walk, National, club 5 Miles Road race, Brighton Relay), the summer track programme, a possible Club Coach and a welcome to new members, with entries to the Asst. Hon. Sec. The Cross Country season has now reached the stage when our lads must test their strength against other clubs in the various open championships. The South of Thames "Senior" race is this year being held at Horsham, and I am sure a most popular result would be a win for that evergreen "youngster," Tommy Marchant, of the local Blue Star Harriers. As regards the team race, this seems very open, although the Navy boys should be dangerous. Although we have to find a new team this year, our newcomers are shaping into a very useful lot, and I fully expect them to put up a good show. Anyway, I hope our supporters will travel to Horsham on 13th February, and give the lads every encouragement. On the 20th we are due to travel to Aldershot for a run against the Command runners, and look forward to our first visit to their headquarters. For those who cannot make the journey we have a social run at Wimbledon with our old friends the Herne Hill Harriers. February 27th—Southern Counties Day.—Both the Senior and Junior races will be held at Farningham—or as it is better known, Horton Kirby, the venue of the Inter-Varsity race. The race was last held here in 1929, when the old war-horse, Bill Cotterell, won the individual race. The course can be termed ideal cross-country, and should prove a test for the best. In the Junior race we should figure prominently and with K. N. Wood, A. F. Clements and that very promising newcomer, E. H. Herbert, backed up by W. E. Lucas, E. J. Selby and H. M. Quackenbos, our Junior Captain, we have a more than useful team and are very hopeful of regaining the title which we held in 1935. This last remark also applies to the Senior race, and on the form so far displayed, it should be a titanic struggle between Surrey A.C. and ourselves. The Surrey boys have for the last two years beaten us in this race although each time we have reversed matters in the "National" race. This time, however, I really think we shall do the trick. Our team is definitely stronger than last season, and should certainly "pack" better than in previous years. You will not regret a journey to Farningham on the 27th, and will see the cream of the Southern runners in a great battle for supremacy. For those of our members who can find the time to make these trips I should like to remind them of the R.W.A. Junior Championship at Leicester on March 6th. I am sure our walkers would welcome the same measure of support that the runners receive. "NATIONAL" DAY, March 13th. Venue: Stratford-on-Avon. Already we have been announced as "National champions," so I trust our lads will justify that optimism. The Birchfield team appears to be up to the strength of previous years, and with their wonderful record in this race, that should speak for itself. The point to remember, however, is that with Pat Parker, Les Cohen and Dan Patience, back from his sojourn in Egypt, we have three men who were not in last year's race. With these men to support Arthur Penny, Bert Footer and Tom Carter, not forgetting Jim Ginty, it would be a super-pessimist who would foreshadow our defeat. It will certainly require some wonderful packing on Birchfield's part to produce a scoring six equal to ours; and as this appears to be Surrey's unlucky race I predict a Belgrave victory with every confidence. I hope we shall have a good crowd of supporters travelling to Stratford-on-Avon. Particulars of train, etc., will be posted at the "Rising Sun," or can be had on application to the Hon. Sec. On the following Saturday, March 20th, we entertain Aldershot Command Harriers on their first visit to Wimbledon. This should give those members who have not run the previous week a chance of an outing, as it will be an all-to-score affair. April 3rd is the day of our 5 Miles Road race with a sealed Handicap in conjunction. We use this race as a basis for selection of our Brighton Relay team and I trust we shall see a good turn-out of our road men. For those whose hopes do not fly so high may I remind them of the Handicap? This will be their last chance during the Winter season. So will all those who have been trying to "work their mark" (I won't mention names) turn out on the 3rd and see what you can do! April 17th—BRIGHTON RELAY DAY. At least that was the date Joe Binks informed us it would be held on, and so far we have not heard of any alteration. What the course is going to be (by this I mean whether it will be the old Brighton main road, or the new course used last year) remains to be discovered. Last year's was far from satisfactory, but our sympathies are all with Joe in the troubles and difficulties he has to contend with in a race of this description. Come what may, I hope we shall continue to be the first team into Brighton. Remember the "locals" are getting used to us by now, and any other result would probably cause a great panic in the town. Also, remember our Pat may one day decide to return to the scenes of his former "triumphs," and as a member of the victorious Belgrave team will probably receive the freedom of the town! Any other result on the 17th may have disastrous effects to our curly-haired "broth of a spalpeen"! As in previous years the Club will have the usual Supporters' buses on the road. We charge 5/- for the return journey, and with the excitement of the race en route, together with a few hours by the sea before our return to Town, I think you will agree that you get your money's worth. For those who would like to put down their names in advance, will they please apply, together with cash, to Alf. Harley, who is the usual charge d'affaires on such occasions. With the Brighton Relay over, the Winter season, so far as the runners are concerned, comes to an end; and we begin to get our track shoes smartened up for the forthcoming Summer season. This year owing to the dressing rooms at Battersea Park being reconstructed (a job which we understand will not be finished until the end of May,) we are forced to make a change in venues for our first two track meetings. We have booked Tooting Bec Track for May 12th, and May 22nd. The former is, of course, "Coronation Day" but I think an evening meeting on this date should be popular with our members. The usual Inter-Club relays with Croydon H., Mitcham A.C. and Epsom H. will also be held on one of these dates; and I hope our members will make it their duty to give Harry Shields and Les Bennett the support that is necessary for us to retain our hold on the Inter-Club Relay Shield. Other fixtures during May include our usual visit to Drayton Green Track for the Inter-Club match with Ealing Harriers, this being on the 8th. Then on the 15th we travel to Broomfield Park for a four-cornered contest with Southgate H., Blackheath H., Polytechnic H. and ourselves. The local club are making arrangements for this meeting to be part of the Borough's Coronation celebrations, so I hope we shall be able to field a much stronger team than that which made the journey last season. We have once again received an invitation to compete in the "Kinnaird" Trophy competition which will be held at the Polytechnic Harriers' meeting at the White City on May 29th. Among the fixtures already arranged are visits to Battersea Park of the Leigh-on-Sea H. and Imperial College A.C. on June 9th, while on July 31st, the London Athletic Club will be our opponents. They expressed a wish to come once again to Battersea Park, and we are very pleased to welcome them. The Club Championships have been fixed for Saturday, July 3rd. This is earlier than has been usual in past years, but it was thought that if our championships were decided before the A.A.A. General Championships, we should have a much better line on which to work when considering the men we should enter for the National Championships. It is also hoped that the earlier date will ensure larger entries for all the events, as many of our members are compelled to accept August Bank Holiday week for their annual vacation. In fact, we are confidently expecting this Club Championship day to be the most successful of the long series, and the earlier date to be a commendable innovation. The thorny question of a Club Coach has been considered by your Committee; and we are very hopeful of securing the services of an old-time member who, we feel sure, would meet our requirements in this connection. Coaches are few and far between. The few well-known are already heavily booked up with various clubs, and if we can secure a man whose services will be exclusive to our own members, I am sure this will prove more satisfactory than having a man who has training interests in, at least, half-a-dozen clubs. Just a few words to new members. If you feel that you are not getting acquainted with your fellow-members as readily as you would like, please do me a favour and drop me a line and I will do my best to remedy that state of affairs. Once you get to know our boys I am sure you will agree that a better set of chaps could not be found elsewhere, so don't get that "out in the cold" feeling. Get in touch with the Asst. Hon. Sec. at once, without delay. All entries and enquiries to: E. A. DUFFETT, Asst. Hon. Sec., 10, Barrow Road, Waddon, Surrey. This time individual victory went to Harry Churcher—to whom our heartiest congraulations. Unfortunately, the support accorded to him on this occasion was not of the best, and the "Berman" Cup passed into the hands of Surrey W.C. Success in the handicap rarely comes our way in the early part of the season and perhaps this is an advantage, for our walkers have a long and arduous season these days, with plenty of—maybe too much—racing. items.s: OUR OPEN WALK. Report of Belgrave's 17th annual open walk at Wimbledon, with 150 entries: V. W. Stone (Poly) won from Harry Churcher, Woodford Green A.C. won the scratch team race by one point, L. J. Wells took the individual handicap, with full result (as printed, P. G. Wright's and W. G. True's handicap times do not equal actual time minus start; the text gives the team handicap to Surrey Walking Club, the results the scratch team to Surrey W.C. under swapped headings). One hundred and fifty entries were received for our 17th annual promotion at Wimbledon, and this must be considered very satisfactory when compared with entries for similar races elsewhere. Of the 150, 28 were Belgrave Harriers, constituting four teams, which shows that our own walkers gave their best support. Our President started the race, and it was soon obvious that there would be a terrific struggle for scratch team honours. The positions fluctuated continually and it was only in the last few yards that Woodford Green A.C. could be sure of a win over Surrey W.C., and then only by one point. Our team was only a further five points away, and as our fourth man actually finished in front of Woodford's fourth, the keen nature of the struggle for team honours can easily be realised. Individually, Stone, of the Poly. Harriers, defeated our Harry Churcher by a yard, with A. A. Cooper third, over two minutes away. The individual handicap went to L. J. Wells, of Surrey W.C., and a second-claim member of our club, with an allowance of 5 min. 30 sec. His actual finishing position was 13th, and on this occasion it could not be regarded as unlucky! Joe Coleman (11th) took second handicap prize, and Harry Churcher was placed third, with the assistance of a one-minute allowance. Despite the fact that our "A" team had two of the three placed men in the individual handicap, they were unplaced in the team handicap. Victory here went to Surrey Walking Club, our "D" team through the efforts of Messrs. Boddington, Clark, Earle, and Jarvis, being second. Fifteen of the first 52 to finish the course were Belgrave Harriers, which is a splendid indication of good all-round strength. The prize for the first Belgrave Harrier not gaining any other award went to Len Fletcher, and a similar prize for M.P.A.A. members was won by Jack Bidgood. In conclusion, we should like to express the Club's grateful thanks to those who helped the promotion along. We are particularly indebted to Messrs. Askew, Bellfield, Gordon and Thomson for generous donations to the Prize Fund; to Mr. Allen for providing one of the prizes; and to the R.W.A. officials, and the competitors whose annual help and support is much appreciated. items.s: THE "JUNIOR" CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the club's junior walking championship for the Horwood Cup on December 12th, won by C. H. Speechley, with the sealed handicap to Len Coleman (as printed, W. G. True's handicap time does not equal actual time minus start). December 12th was a miserable day, but considering the number of "Seniors" we now have in our ranks not eligible to compete for the "Horwood" Cup, the entry must be considered satisfactory. There were some walkers missing that we should have liked to see in action, and curtailment of Police leave due to the special calls of this time, robbed us of all but one of our Police members. Joe Coleman took the lead at the start, but was ruled out after a mile, when he had a fifteen yards advantage over Charlie Speechley. The oldest junior in the race stayed in front for the remainder of the race, being content to do this and return slow time. Douglas Earle walked splendidly and his fastest race yet to take second position; with George Boddington repeating his good walking of our "Open" event and being placed third. The sealed handicap went to Len Coleman, who shows improvement every time out, and will be with the leaders before long. Earle claimed second award, and Bill Snell the third prize. J. A. Bellchambers, son of our Past President, made his dêbut in this race, and as he matures physically will undoubtedly prove himself as valuable to future teams as his father was to past Belgrave teams. items.label: February 1937
items.sum: Walking notes: the Boxing Day Croydon to Godstone and back race, the Surrey W.C. v. Belgrave match over the West Wickham course, and coming fixtures including the "Junior" Championship at Leicester, the club 20 miles for the R. W. Ricketts Shield and the National 20 miles near Epsom.
e: Croydon to Godstone and back walk
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes: the Boxing Day Croydon to Godstone and back race, the Surrey W.C. v. Belgrave match over the West Wickham course, and coming fixtures including the "Junior" Championship at Leicester, the club 20 miles for the R. W. Ricketts Shield and the National 20 miles near Epsom. Five of our walkers paid Christmas penance and walked in the Boxing Day Croydon to Godstone and back race of 18¾ miles. Charlie Churcher, our Captain, distinguished himself by finishing third in his first attempt at this distance, being only 2 mins. 23 secs. behind the winner, D. Christie-Murray, of Surrey W.C. Jack Bidgood also did well to finish fifth on his initial walk over this course. Times, etc., of our men were: 3rd, C. Churcher, 2h. 40m. 28s.; 5th, J. Bidgood, 2h. 43m. 16s.; 14th, D. E. Brown, 2h. 57m. 37s.; 15th, W. H. Snell, 2h. 57m. 52s.; 16th, A. A. Harley, 2h. 57m. 55s. Our team was second in the scratch event; and won the handicap team race, the successful trio consisting of Messrs. Bidgood, Churcher and Snell. * * * * * On December 5th we made our usual visit to Croydon, to oppose Surrey W.C. over their West Wickham and back course of 9¾ miles. We had fourteen walkers present, probably our best attendance yet for this race, and had hopes of winning the inter-club race for the first time. Harry Churcher walked wonderfully well to win, by nearly a minute from Astill, of the home team. Then came C. E. Churcher and J. C. Bidgood, and with three in four we had made an excellent start. Unfortunately for us, our packing was not so good in the middle portion of the race, and eventually our Surrey friends claimed a win, scoring 163 points to our 188. So ended a very close and exciting race. With the assistance of Len Fletcher, Joe Coleman and Jack Rutland, who were prevented from turning out, it would have been even closer and we should probably have claimed a win. However, away with "might-have-beens," congratulations and thanks to our good friends of the Surrey Walking Club! * * * * * On February 20th Valentine's S.C. hold their Open 10 Miles race at Chadwell Heath, and this will be the last try-out before the "Junior" Championship. This event has now taken the date formerly reserved to Ashcombe A.C., who promoted instead a seven miles race a month earlier. * * * * * March 6th is "Junior" Championship day, and the race takes place at Leicester. At the time of writing it is hard to weigh up the chances of the teams, but it certainly seems a very open race. After our win of last year, and the necessity of finding a new scoring team, our own chances of winning again would be ignored by most outside critics. Additionally, we are disappointed that Reg. Elson, E. C. Heather and L. Storey, all experienced "Junior" racing men, have not been able to train regularly this year, but we hope to have their assistance next year. Despite the foregoing, we are far from being out of the race, and a sound team will represent the Club. We should most certainly maintain our excellent record in this race and take a place; and with a little luck (or should we write "if the team can rise to the occasion") we may well find ourselves winners for the sixth time. Anyway, we can be sure the team will do credit to the Club, and so "Best of Luck!" * * * * * The County Walking Championships take place on March 20th, and a week later the Inter-counties team race will be held at Horsham. * * * * * The Club 20 Miles championship for the "R. W. Ricketts" Shield, and sealed handicap in conjunction, will be held on April 24th. A match versus Metropolitan Police W.C. will also add interest. * * * * * The National title over 20 miles will be contested in the Epsom neighbourhood, the grandstand being used as dressing accommodation. What are our prospects of taking the Championship from Surrey Walking Club? Time alone will show, but we are certain our team will not spare themselves in their endeavours to regain the title. items.s: SOCIAL MATTERS. Social notes for the club's Jubilee Year: the Golden Jubilee Dinner and Dance at the Quadrant Restaurant on May 1st, a dance at Queensberry Hall on February 20th and a social at Wimbledon on April 3rd. Nobody needs reminding that this year is the Club's Jubilee Year, and that no effort should be spared to make 1937 the most successful year in Belgravian history. Those responsible for the organisation of the social side hope that every member will support the various social functions during Jubilee Year, and make them occasions to be remembered for many years to come. The most important social function is the Golden Jubilee Dinner and Dance that will be held on May 1st at the Quadrant Restaurant, Regent Street, W.1. This venue must be convenient for everyone, being within one minute's walk of Piccadilly Circus. It is hoped to make this affair a really outstanding occasion, with as many as possible present. Dancing will follow the Dinner and, for the convenience of those who so desire, our Social Hon. Secretary and his assistants have arranged to accept payment by instalments during the month or two preceding the function, so that the expense will not fall too heavily on one week's income. This is a facility which all (and Hon. Editors in particular, I can assure you) should find most helpful. Our next Dance takes place at the Queensberry Hall, South Kensington, on February 20th. Our New Year's Eve Dance at this Hall can be written down as a great success, and we are confident that those who paid taxi fares home, or who were late to work in the morning, can have no regrets. A further Social at Wimbledon has been arranged for April 3rd. Note the date. All enquiries and applications for tickets to: A. E. TAYLOR, 11, Fitzneal Street, W.12. A. E. Taylor A. E. items.sum: The Hon. Treasurer thanks members for gifts on his marriage and explains when club subscriptions fall due.
items.s: THE HON. TREASURER'S NOTES. The Hon. Treasurer thanks members for gifts on his marriage and explains when club subscriptions fall due. Firstly, I desire to express my appreciation of the very kind wishes and thoughts tendered to me on the occasion of my marriage. I thank you also for the very serviceable and attractive clock presented to me; a most desirable article which will not only enable me to keep pace with the times, but will serve as a constant reminder of the many happy years that the Club has given me. It is on occasions such as this that one can readily be persuaded to believe that there is, after all, little or no wisdom in the Immortal advice of Punch. Secondly, I should like to thank all those members who so kindly responded to my circular letter regarding subscriptions. As to those who have not already done so, I feel sure I can count on that spirit of steadfast loyalty that has always animated them and may expect to hear from them shortly together with, of course, the requisite enclosure. Whilst on the subject of subscriptions, there appears to exist among members some misunderstanding as to when subscriptions become payable. Some members believe that the date of payment is governed by the date of their election to the Club. Others believe that payment is only at such times as they are inclined to athletic activity; whilst apart from those who habitually leave payment until the close of the season, there are those who genuinely believe that payment is not due until this time, assuming that the Annual General Meeting marks the close of the season. Actually the 15th September of each year is the date on which the Club Financial year closes, and the A.G.M. which takes place on the last Tuesday of that month marks the opening of the new season. In any case, however, the subscription is required to be paid once only and in this connection I would draw the attention of all members to the Club Rules (which this year are printed in the Club Handbook) with particular reference to rule 9 (a), which states that all subscriptions become due and payable on the date of the Annual General Meeting. And now there may be a few members who have not received my circular regarding outstanding subscriptions. This may be for one of two reasons, or both. (1) Change of address and failure to notify the Club. (2) Being in arrears of subscription for the past season. To those under (1) I would suggest that they communicate with me at once. To those under (2) I am writing, and in all probability my letter will be in their hands before this Gazette is published. It will be appreciated, and it will certainly lighten the duties of Club officials, if these members will kindly reply to this letter indicating one way or other their attitude as to membership having regard to the conditions of Rule 9, paras. a, b, c, e. The record of the Club is unique and the Committee recognise with satisfaction the great position which members have won for themselves, and the Club in the world of athletics generally. It needs, however, strenuous effort and the close co-operation of all in all the many obligations if this high standard is to be maintained. The payment of subscription when due is no less important an obligation than any other. W. G. WEBB, Hon. Treasurer. W. G. Webb W. G. WEBB Hon. Treasurer; thanks members for good wishes and a clock presented on his marriage W. G. WEBB

items.label: February 1937
items.h: A GREAT OPPORTUNITY FOR BELGRAVE SPRINTERS.
items.sum: The Track Vice-Captain urges Belgrave sprinters to train regularly together and build team spirit for the relay races.
items.s: A GREAT OPPORTUNITY FOR BELGRAVE SPRINTERS. The Track Vice-Captain urges Belgrave sprinters to train regularly together and build team spirit for the relay races. It is with a great deal of regret that I feel I am compelled to write this short article. In the past the performances of our sprinters have been mediocre. What are the reasons? In my opinion the reasons are:— (a) Lack of regular and systematic training; (b) A certain lack of team-spirit. Let me make it quite clear that I am not in any way referring to the small band of sprinters who, last season, gave their whole-hearted support when called upon by the Club to run in team events. The individual performances of these loyal Club-men show that the experience gained in the team races has proved invaluable. I would like to see the sprinters self-supporting; that is, carry through in the various relay races entirely with sprinters, and not borrow runners who favour longer distances. Sprinters! You can make your training a real pleasure by getting together and training together, thus creating and conserving the real Club atmosphere which is so vitally necessary to the well-being and even life of the Belgrave Harriers. Competition for places in the Club's sprint teams should be really keen; and all of you should have the enthusiasm which goes to make just an ordinary team on paper into a winning team in practice. The WILL TO WIN is needed. The talent is in all of you and can be brought out by training with your colleagues in a regular and systematic manner. All sprinters in the Club have this year a great opportunity of winning for Belgrave, in its Golden Jubilee Year, some of the highest honours on the track. So please take this article as "a call to action," and turn out in your dozens in the approaching track season. Seniors! encourage the Juniors. In conclusion, let me wish you every success and happiness in the future! L. G. Bennett L. G. BENNETT Track Vice-Captain L. G. BENNETT

items.label: February 1937
items.sum: Frank Simmons backs Les Bennett's appeal, arguing that Belgrave sprinters need regular training together more than a professional coach.
items.s: TO SPRINTERS. Frank Simmons backs Les Bennett's appeal, arguing that Belgrave sprinters need regular training together more than a professional coach. Frank Simmons writes on similar lines to Les Bennett above and says: "The comparative weakness of our sprinters has been referred to in previous issues of 'The Belgravian,' and it has been suggested that the Club employs the services of a coach. Whilst favouring this, one wonders 'Is it worth while?' From personal observation last season, I noticed a well-known coach concentrating on one Olympic possible, and neglecting the others! Of what good is this? "Our cross-country men have not needed a professional coach, and yet have given us a series of sterling performances. The secret of this success is, no doubt, regularity in training, and concerted training. If the sprinters really mean to do well, they must train together in the same way. In the past they have turned up at all sorts of times, and so invariably trained alone, with the tendency to do either too much or too little." "If we are sincere in our desire to change all this, let us respond to Les Bennett's appeal and 'get together.' Then we shall really become a force to be reckoned with in all classes of sprint events." Frank Simmons Frank Simmons writes on sprint training Les Bennett Les Bennett his appeal to sprinters to train together

items.label: June 1937
items.sum: Editorial notes on a Jubilee Year of near-misses, congratulating Jim Ginty on his International cross-country race and Harry Churcher on his A.A.A. 7 miles walk second, with news of Harry Shields' marriage, the Littlehampton outing, early track matches and a welcome to new members.
items.s: Editorial notes on a Jubilee Year of near-misses, congratulating Jim Ginty on his International cross-country race and Harry Churcher on his A.A.A. 7 miles walk second, with news of Harry Shields' marriage, the Littlehampton outing, early track matches and a welcome to new members. Our Jubilee Year seems to have been accompanied by more than a little misfortune. Although, generally, our fortunes are at a higher level than they have ever been before, various small influences seem to have affected us and prevented that super-excellence of performance which we should have liked to have associated with our Jubilee Year. Despite our minor disappointments, our record during the Championship season remains a very fine one, and we feel safe in saying that the Club's continued all-round excellence surpasses anything to be seen elsewhere now, or in past records. After virtually winning the Southern, only to have the race declared void—a right decision, let it be said—we secured second place in both "National" and "Brighton" Relays, details of which appear elsewhere. Our walkers have been placed third in both "Junior" and "Senior" Championships, and this sums up the results of our Winter training by both runners and walkers. These results possess real merit, but we have it in us to do a little better and, with just the slightest of smiles from Dame Fortune, we shall undoubtedly do so next season. * * * * * Heartiest congratulations to Jim Ginty, the first Belgrave man to be placed in the English Cross-Country Championships, and upon his subsequent selection for the English team. Further congratulations upon finishing third in the International race at Brussels, and leading home the English team to a splendid win. * * * * * Congratulations also to Harry Churcher upon finishing second in the A.A.A. 7 miles Walk Championship. His was the luck to follow home Mickaelsson, of Sweden, who set up a new World's record of 50 mins. 19 1-5 secs. Harry's time was 51 mins. 13 secs., which was faster than any previous winning Championship time! And this particular Championship goes back to 1866! Well walked, Harry! * * * * * Heartiest good wishes to our Track Captain, Harry Shields, on the occasion of his recent marriage. We wish Mr. and Mrs. Shields many years of happily married life. * * * * * Details are given elsewhere of a Club Outing to Littlehampton on Sunday, July 4th. Your Social Hon. Secretary would be glad to know as soon as possible if you intend going, so that he can make the necessary arrangements. Give him your support and let him know at the very earliest possible moment. * * * * * Our Track season has commenced and already we have participated in several matches. At the Southgate Coronation Meeting we were placed third of the four competing clubs, our field events men gathering many points for us. Final scores were: Southgate H., 37 pts., Blackheath H. 34½ pts., Belgrave H. 25½ pts. Polytechnic H. 24 pts. In the first of the inter-club relays between Mitcham A.C., Epsom H., Croydon H. and ourselves, we started well by winning all four events. Our participation in the "Kinnaird Trophy" competition was barren of points, but several of our runners did well in this high standard of competition. Detailed reports of this meeting and others are held over to our next issue. * * * * * A special word of welcome to all those new members who have joined our ranks recently. Make yourself known, enjoy the benefits of the Club to the full, and don't hesitate to ask or write for advice or information to any of the Club officials whose names appear on the fixture list. They are only too willing to assist the newcomer. And so, the best of luck to all our new friends! items.s: THE "JUBILEE" DINNER. Report of the Club Jubilee Dinner and Dance at the Quadrant Restaurant, Regent Street, on 1 May, with the toasts and speakers. Over two hundred guests, friends and members attended the Club Jubilee Dinner and Dance, held at The Quadrant Restaurant, Regent Street, on Saturday, May 1st. The function was most successful and our congratulations and thanks are due to our Social Hon. Secretary, A. E. Taylor, for his efforts on our behalf. A special souvenir menu card, in Club colours, had been provided, containing a short history of the Club's fifty years of existence. After dinner, our President gave the Loyal Toast, and later proposed "The Club" in a short but pointed speech. W. H. Hare responded in fitting terms, and referred to the Club's progress in past years. A. A. Harley expressed the Club's pleasure at the presence of so many well-known guests and gave the toast of "The Visitors." Entertaining responses were made by Mr. L. N. Richardson (Hon. Sec., English Cross-Country Union, who had travelled from Derby to be present; and by Mr. F. Gordon Brown, President of the Middlesex County A.A.A. J. C. Bidgood then proposed the health of "Our President," which was vociferously honoured, and "Wally" made a short speech of thanks before closing the first part of our "Jubilee" function. When tables and chairs were cleared, dancing was enjoyed until midnight, when all joined in "Auld Lang Syne," and went their way, vowing this important and historic Club function to have been a great success. items.sum: L. G. Bennett announces a 24-second standard for the Club 220 yards Championship and an extra 220 yards handicap, and urges sprinters to train together, race in handicaps and wear the Club vest.
items.s: TO THE SPRINTERS. L. G. Bennett announces a 24-second standard for the Club 220 yards Championship and an extra 220 yards handicap, and urges sprinters to train together, race in handicaps and wear the Club vest. In an endeavour to make our sprinters show more enthusiasm than has sometimes been exhibited in recent years, the Committee has fixed a standard time of 24 secs. in the Club 220 yards Championship. All sprinters beating this time, excluding the first three, will receive the Club bronze standard medal. Please note also that an extra 220 yards handicap has been included in this year's track fixtures. I should like to make a further appeal to our sprinters to get together, to train together and to support the efforts of the Committee to strengthen our sprinting section. Most men can make themselves fitter by persistent training. The fitter the man, the more likely he is to score for the Club when called upon in match events. The number of points scored by our sprinters in recent years in match events have been small, and it is up to us to remedy this. Every sprinter should support the Club programme of handicaps. Valuable experience can be gained in these events, and it has been proved that plenty of racing is necessary if a sprinter is to improve. Discuss your problems with your Club-mates. Exchange views for the common good. And don't forget to fix upon a plan of training. Let "Little and often" be your motto. Also, don't forget those body exercises, and the help that can be obtained from the books on Athletics in the local library. New members are asked to come forward and ask for the Captains or Vice-Captains; and all Club-members are requested to wear the Club vest in racing and in training, when it becomes easier to get together and train together. If you are without a Club vest, this is easily remedied. Just see our Hon. Treasurer, Bill Webb. Finally, I would ask all our supporters to turn up at home and away fixtures. Vocal encouragement can help a lot, and additionally, you can often learn something from the stylish running of one of our opponents in the match events. And so, best of luck to you all! L. G. Bennett L. G. BENNETT L. G. BENNETT Bill Webb Bill Webb Hon. Treasurer Club 220 yards Championship

items.label: June 1937
items.sum: Junior notes on the new Club Junior Championships, county, Southern and A.A.A. junior championships, F. J. Skelley's Loughborough scholarship, W. E. Lucas's Brighton relay stage, and training nights at Battersea Park.
items.s: WITH THE JUNIORS. Junior notes on the new Club Junior Championships, county, Southern and A.A.A. junior championships, F. J. Skelley's Loughborough scholarship, W. E. Lucas's Brighton relay stage, and training nights at Battersea Park. One of the welcome innovations which mark our Jubilee Year is the institution of Club Junior Championships. Hitherto only a 100 yards (under 15) and a 220 yards (under 18) have been included, but this year, in addition to the former event, we have races at 100, 220 and 880 yards for those under the age of 19. Also the number of junior handicap events has been increased to suit sprinters and middle-distance runners. You can't expect to get picked for our teams if you're not known to club officials—if you turn out in these handicaps we can get some idea of your form. The numerous club handicaps at all distances give further opportunities for enjoyable competition. Any club official will take entries for these events. Now a word or two about various outside championships. Middlesex members are lucky in that their County holds a track and field meeting for those under 19 and several events are included with a sixteen years age limit. In addition to the place medals, standard medals are awarded in every event except the short sprint. Surrey hold only a 100 yards race and an 880 yards race in conjunction with their Senior Championships on June 5th. These championships will have been decided by the time you read these words. The Southern Junior Championships are being held at Ladywell Park on June 19th and here again standard medals are awarded in both track and field events. We hope to enter a team in the 4 x 110 yards relay. Our outstanding performers should make a point of training up for the A.A.A. Junior Championship, to take place on July 10th, at the White City. Last year the reward of one of our long-jumpers, F. J. Skelley (who finished a close second in this event) was a scholarship to the Summer School at Loughborough. Many cannot hope to do so well, but it is worth while to enter for the sake of gaining a standard medal. A note for the field event men: we haven't a separate section for the juniors, but all our jumpers, throwers and putters, of all ages and abilities, train together, and any junior will be welcomed into this mystic sect. Lastly, congratulations to W. E. Lucas, still a junior under cross-country ruling, who ran a fine stage at a critical period in the recent London-Brighton relay. Enquiries to H. M. QUACKENBOS, at Battersea Park, or to 34, Eaton Terrace, S.W.1. All newcomers are asked to make themselves known to the Club officials, when arrangements for training, etc., can be discussed, introductions effected and the new man made familiar with Club procedure. items.label: June 1937
items.sum: Field events notes appealing for members, thanking Mr. Daily for cups for the Long Jump and Javelin Championships, and setting standard-medal marks for the Club championships.
items.s: FIELD EVENTS. Field events notes appealing for members, thanking Mr. Daily for cups for the Long Jump and Javelin Championships, and setting standard-medal marks for the Club championships. The Summer Season is here again, and we should like all field events men to rally round once again as in past years, and to see some new recruits to our branch of Athletics. We are very grateful to Mr. Daily, who has presented the Club with two handsome cups, which have been allocated to the Long Jump and Javelin Championships. It is to be hoped that all our Field Event Championships will eventually be provided with trophies. Meanwhile the Committee have decided to award standard medals in connection with the Club championships as follows: Long Jump, 19ft. 3in.; High Jump, 5ft. 1in.; Javelin, 115ft.; Shot Putt, 31ft.; Discus, 85ft. These medals will be awarded on the same condition as those given for track events. It is to be hoped that more of our men will be successful in winning the Club Honours Badge. Constant training and determination will ensure success. A pleasing feature of the early matches this season has been the help given by our section. This was particularly noticeable in the match at Southgate, when our field events men gathered the majority of the Club points. One last word. If invited to turn out for the Club and unable to do so, please advise me to return of post. Your help in this will be greatly appreciated. All enquiries should be sent to: G. H. items.label: June 1937
items.sum: Report and result of the R.W.A. Junior Championship at Leicester on 6 March, won by Metropolitan W.C. from Surrey W.C., with a Belgrave team of new men placing third and nine finishing in 47 places; the winner's club is printed "London Vid. W..C." in the result and London Vidarians W.C. appears in the team placings.
items.s: THE R.W.A. JUNIOR CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the R.W.A. Junior Championship at Leicester on 6 March, won by Metropolitan W.C. from Surrey W.C., with a Belgrave team of new men placing third and nine finishing in 47 places; the winner's club is printed "London Vid. W..C." in the result and London Vidarians W.C. appears in the team placings. Last year, at Hendon, it will be remembered that we scored a very fine win over Leicester W.C. in this championship, and consequently, in accordance with the rules, we were compelled to draw on other men this year. Our team did well to be placed third in this year's race, held at Leicester, and we may expect even better things next year. March 6th was the chosen date and although some of our members who have demonstrated their worth in previous "Juniors" were unable to train and compete, we knew that we had a sound team capable of adding to our long list of placings in this championship. A fairly stiff course had been selected with a particularly steep hill to negotiate round about the seven miles mark. From the start Metropolitan W.C., the favourites, were prominent, and with the disqualification of some of the principal Leicester walkers, it was soon evident that the team race would be fought out between three London clubs—the Metropolitan W.C., Surrey W.C. and ourselves. Suffolk R.W.A. threatened danger at one point, but in the closing miles their chances faded. At seven miles the Metropolitan W.C. had five men in the first seventeen places, and it was evident that they would win if they could last out. This they succeeded in doing and scored their first Championship win, with Surrey Walking Club trying hard to peg them back, taking second place. Meanwhile our walkers had raced with splendid judgment, the majority gaining places over the last three miles. Colin Sutton and Joe Coleman did very well to take such forward positions; and no one will begrudge Len Coleman the praise and congratulations he received on finishing 18th. Starting last October, he has progressed at a remarkable rate and in splendid form; and next year we shall expect him to be right in front. Bill Snell came through well over the last three miles to complete our team and ensure third place for the Club. Our next man to finish was Stan Goold (31st), followed by a very promising newcomer, Syd English (32nd). In all we finished nine men in 47 places—a most satisfying performance, particularly in view of the fact that last year's team was no longer eligible, and that the year following a win is usually a difficult one for team-building. This occasion was the fourteenth in 18 post-war years, in which we have been placed; and in five championships we have had the satisfaction of taking the winning medals—a record superior to that of any other club. Next year will find us with an excellent chance of adding to this splendid record. This year's result is appended, and if all our men can improve a few positions we may well have the race to ourselves! m. s. 1 R. Sims (London Vid. W..C.) 81 59 2 G. items.s: THE CLUB 20 MILES WALK CHAMPIONSHIP. Report and result of the Club 20 Miles Walk Championship for the R. W. Rickett's Shield, won by C. E. Churcher, with A. A. Harley taking the sealed handicap and Belgrave beating the Metropolitan Police in the match by 67 points to 73. In connection with the Club Championship for the "R. W. Rickett's Shield" and sealed handicap, a match had been arranged with the Metropolitan Police, and accordingly a large field started out. The invitation of our course, to retire from the race at 8, 11 or 17 miles, was accepted by many, however, and less than half the starters completed the course. The holder, F. Rickards, was unable to compete. Charlie Churcher, Jack Bidgood and Fred Bentley set the pace early on. Pope, Fletcher and Wright preferred to start comparatively slowly, and speed up as the race progressed. Churcher walked strongly throughout and dropping his opponents, won fairly easily from Bidgood and Bentley, who were to fight out the Police Long Distance Championship on the following Thursday. Towards the end, Bob Readman, who had been prominent early on, fell back slightly, and Fletcher and Pope made up places. Percy Wright walked well at his first attempt, but was leg-weary towards the end and was passed by Harley, who won the sealed handicap. As the result shows, Belgrave had a slight advantage over the Police in the match. The Club handicap must receive the "official" blessing, for it was won by the Walk Hon. items.label: June 1937
items.sum: Report and result of the National 20 Miles Walk Championship from Epsom grandstand, won by S. A. Fletcher (Derbyshire S.C.), with Leicester W.C. and Surrey W.C. dead-heating for the team title and a weakened Belgrave team third; J. C. Bidgood earned the Club Honours Badge.
items.s: THE NATIONAL 20 MILES WALK. Report and result of the National 20 Miles Walk Championship from Epsom grandstand, won by S. A. Fletcher (Derbyshire S.C.), with Leicester W.C. and Surrey W.C. dead-heating for the team title and a weakened Belgrave team third; J. C. Bidgood earned the Club Honours Badge. This year's Championship was held from Epsom grandstand, over a severe three-lap course. We had hopes of regaining the Championship, but last-minute disappointments robbed us of our chances. It had been intended that Bidgood, Bentley, C. E. Churcher, Fletcher, Green, Harley, Readman and Rickards, should be our team. Unfortunately, Fletcher was indisposed, Green was unable to turn out, and Rickards was also compelled to stand down at the last moment. Harley was unfortunate enough to catch a severe cold a few days prior to the race; and generally the misfortunes which seem to have followed all the Club's activities in our Jubilee Year, persisted. F. H. Elson, E. Saunders and S. C. Roberts were promoted to fill the vacant three places in the "A" team. A "B" team, consisting of Boddington, Clark, Cornish, Martin, Snell, Reeve and Sutton also started. From the start our walkers were prominent, together with those of Surrey W.C. and Leicester W.C.—the three teams securing the placings in last year's race. It was soon obvious that our need for a strong fourth man was great, and we should have been very grateful for a fit Rickards or Green in our ranks! Bentley, Bidgood and Churcher were doing well near the front; and Readman, our fourth man, tried manfully to give them the needed support. The end came, however, with Leicester W.C. and Surrey W.C. dead-heating for the Championship, with our team, once again, third. This must be considered creditable in view of our last-minute disappointments. Meanwhile, our congratulations go to Surrey W.C. who, at least, did not lose their title; and to Leicester W.C. upon securing joint winning brackets for the first time. Of our team there can be nothing but praise for the efforts of Bentley, Churcher and Bidgood, who finished 9th, 10th and 12th, scoring 28 points between them. Our fourth man, as last year, was Bob Readman, scoring 28, who did well over such a hilly course. Roberts, competing in his first big race for us, was 44th, Harley 57th and Ted Saunders 68th. Frank Elson was compelled to retire from the race. So much for our "A" team men. Of the "B" team, Colin Sutton did extremely well to finish 32nd, and thus show up our team selection! Colin had been forced to retire in the Club Championship a fornight earlier, with blistered feet. Bob Martin, also walking in the "B" team, (he had been unable to walk in the Club Championship), showed form of a few years back in finishing 36th. E. G. Cornish, of the "B" team finished in 90th position, and as the remainder of this team retired, our "B" team did not close in. We were actually the first Club to finish eight walkers, but as they were not all nominated in one team, the "Nijmegen Shield" went to Surrey W.C., whose eighth "A" team man finished in 52nd scoring position. We must try and sort things out a little better another year! In conclusion, a word of sincere congratulation to the winner, S. A. Fletcher (Derbyshire S.C.) upon a splendid performance over a most difficult course; and to our John Bidgood, whose performance gains for him the coveted Club Honours Badge. 12 teams closed in. h. m. s. 1 S. items.label: June 1937
items.sum: Walking notes on Harry Churcher's A.A.A. 7 miles, Surrey County 10 miles and Inter-Counties successes, the Surrey and Middlesex county championships, the Ashcombe and Valentine's open walks, prospects for the R.W.A. Junior and 20-mile racing, the R.W.A. 50 kilos at Southgate, the Police Barking–Southend walk, and forthcoming club walking events.
items.s: WITH THE WALKERS. Walking notes on Harry Churcher's A.A.A. 7 miles, Surrey County 10 miles and Inter-Counties successes, the Surrey and Middlesex county championships, the Ashcombe and Valentine's open walks, prospects for the R.W.A. Junior and 20-mile racing, the R.W.A. 50 kilos at Southgate, the Police Barking–Southend walk, and forthcoming club walking events. We are all glad to see Harry Churcher accomplish such a fine performance in the A.A.A. 7 Miles Championship. He has had his rebuffs in the past, and we are glad that perseverance and concentration have enabled him to overcome all obstacles with such good purpose. If he continues to improve at the same rate, World's records will be placed against his name. We must congratulate him upon winning the Surrey County 10 Miles title, and in walking away with the Inter-Counties race the following week. * * * * * In addition to Harry Churcher, the Surrey team contained J. G. Coleman and L. J. Coleman, whilst A. Readman figured in the Middlesex team and S. R. English was a member of the Kent team. * * * * * In the Surrey County Championship we were only able to take second place to Surrey Walking Club, despite H. G. Churcher's individual win. C. E. Churcher and Don Brown suffered disqualification, and although the Coleman brothers walked well, Surrey W.C. won by 33 points to our 50. On the same day, Cadogan A.C. fielded a team in the Middlesex race, all of whom are Belgrave Harriers. Bob Readman (10th) was the first man home and the team, weakened by the absence of several prominent members, finished fourth. * * * * * Appended are the results of the Ashcombe A.C. Open 7 miles race and of the Valentine's S.C. Open 10 miles event. In the former promotion, held for the first time at this distance, we won two sets of team prizes; and Colin Sutton was placed third in the individual handicap. In the race held at Chadwell Heath our "A" team was placed third in the team handicap. * * * * * The results of the R.W.A. "Junior" and "Senior" Championships are given elsewhere, and it is pleasing to think that we can manage to be among the placings year by year in the face of strenuous opposition. * * * * * Next year's "Junior" should give us the chance of fielding a "strongest ever" team. With this year's scoring four, plus E. C. Heather and R. F. Elson, who expect to be able to train regularly next winter, and newcomers, such as English and Roberts available, and others challenging for positions; it should be an embarrassing business to select our first team. * * * * * It is also encouraging to see some of our younger walkers turning their minds towards twenty-miles racing. We should have a team second to none at this distance in a few years' time if this promise is maintained. There is a great fascination about a twenty-miles race. Not only are speed and stamina required, but also that very elusive quality, judgment of pace and ability to spread out one's efforts evenly over the whole distance. It is surprising how often the champion at ten miles is an indifferent performer at double the distance, and how the really "long-distance" man holds his own with his shorter-distance colleague. * * * * * The R.W.A. 50 kilos Championship, which we have held for the past three years, is to be contested from De Bohun's Farm, Southgate, on July 24th. We expect to field a strong team, and the help of a few attendants on the road would be appreciated. * * * * * The Police Barking—Southend Walk over 33 miles 6 furlongs, was very nearly a "Belgrave" triumph, for Fred Bentley was first, Jack Bidgood second, Bob Readman fourth, and S. C. Roberts sixth! We should certainly have won the team race if such things were permitted in a purely Police Walk! * * * * * The track season is now well on us and we wish all our walkers success in the various championship events; and to those who aim lower, success in the handicap events. * * * * * The Club Championships are to be held on an earlier date this year, and the "A. J. Sawyer" Cup will be competed for on Saturday, July 3rd. Two classes of standard are again in operation, and it is to be hoped that we shall have a "bumper" entry. On July 14th we hold a One Mile Walk, open to unattached novices, entry being free. All members are asked to bring this event to the notice of their friends. New members are always very welcome, and this race, with the co-operation of members, may mean the introduction of a future champion to the Club. So please do what you can among your friends and work-mates. All members should now have their fixture cards and be aware of the Club programme. If for any reason, such as change of address, you have not had your fixture card, please notify one of the Club officials. A good programme of handicaps has again been arranged and entries for championship and handicap events should be sent to:— A. A. Harley, 39, Roxborough Avenue, Isleworth, Mx. items.label: June 1937
items.sum: Report by T. J. Flower of the Club 10 Miles Cross Country Championship, run in terrible weather with the Brook in flood, won by Jim Ginty from holder Arthur Penny by about seven yards, with full result and handicap times.
items.s: THE 10 MILES CROSS COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Report by T. J. Flower of the Club 10 Miles Cross Country Championship, run in terrible weather with the Brook in flood, won by Jim Ginty from holder Arthur Penny by about seven yards, with full result and handicap times. Although the weather was terrible, a good field turned out for this event. Arthur Penny, the holder, was looking very fit and confident, as were quite a number of others. It was very pleasing to see nearly all our "stars" turning out and looking really fit. We expected a good race and were not disappointed. As the Brook was in flood, the runners made a lap of the field (nearly a mile) to start, and at the end of this lap it was good to see about 18 runners well bunched together in spite of the fast pace set by Penny, Parker, Taylor and Co. At the half-way mark Penny and Ginty were leading with Parker about 30 yards behind. At this point fifteen runners passed within a minute of the leaders—a very satisfactory state of affairs. The next time we saw the runners was about 400 yards from the finish. A gruelling race was in progress between Penny and Ginty. First one appeared to gain a small advantage, then the other, and they turned into the final straight practically level. Ginty eventually forced himself to the front to win by about seven yards—a splendid race between two very game runners. As the first two finished, Parker entered the finishing straight closely followed by Footer, who had put in some very fast second-half running. The race was a credit to the fitness of all the competitors, and of those making their first attempt, I would particularly mention A. Beaumont. items.h: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES CHAMPIONSHIP.
items.sum: Report of the South of the Thames Championship at Horsham, where Belgrave's young team, weakened by the eligibility rules, finished 11th; with result and team placings.
items.s: THE SOUTH OF THE THAMES CHAMPIONSHIP. Report of the South of the Thames Championship at Horsham, where Belgrave's young team, weakened by the eligibility rules, finished 11th; with result and team placings. This Championship was decided this year at Horsham, and as our last year's winning team was no longer eligible, according to the rules govering this event, our chances of being placed were very small. A difficult course and unpleasant weather conditions, still further handicapped our team, which contained several young and comparatively untried runners. In these circumstances, our team position, although lower than our normal performance in this race, must not be regarded with dissatisfaction. In Clements, Lucas, and the younger Herbert, we have three junior runners destined for the highest rank. Beaumont, Wood and Tobin are all likely to show improved performances next year. We detect plenty of evidence of another winning team in a year or two. As in all races where "barring" clauses operate, a club gradually builds up a team year by year until it becomes a winning team. This team in the act of winning (or of being placed in Southern or English Championships) loses its eligibility, and the business of building a new winning team starts all over again! This, of course, is the purpose of the "junior" championships—to encourage the younger and unknown runners. The race result is appended :— m. s. 1 A. J. Hughes (Reading A.C.) 43 12 49 A. F.
